When in doubt, check the OVN source code for your release. | Table | Name | Purpose | |-------|------|---------| | **44** | **CHK_LB_OUTPUT** | **Loopback prevention - drops packets that would loop back (high volume, normal)** | | 64 | SAVE_INPORT | Save ingress port for later | | 65 | LOG_TO_PHY | Logical to physical mapping | | 66 | MAC_BINDING | MAC binding lookups | | 67 | MAC_LOOKUP | MAC address table lookups | | 68-69 | CHK_LB_HAIRPIN | Load balancer hairpin checks | | 70 | CT_SNAT_HAIRPIN | Conntrack SNAT hairpin | | 71-72 | GET/LOOKUP_FDB | FDB (forwarding DB) lookups | | 73-74 | CHK_IN_PORT_SEC | Ingress port security | | 75 | CHK_OUT_PORT_SEC | Egress port security | | 76-77 | ECMP_NH | ECMP next-hop handling | | 78 | CHK_LB_AFFINITY | Load balancer affinity | | **79** | **MAC_CACHE_USE** | **MAC cache miss (high volume, normal)** | | 80 | CT_ZONE_LOOKUP | Conntrack zone lookup | | 81-83 | CT_ORIG_*_LOAD | Conntrack original tuple loading | | 84 | FLOOD_REMOTE_CHASSIS | Remote chassis flooding | | 85 | CT_STATE_SAVE | Conntrack state save | | 86 | CT_ORIG_PROTO_LOAD | Conntrack protocol loading | | 87 | GET_REMOTE_FDB | Remote FDB lookup | **Relevant drop tables for troubleshooting:** - **Table 9**: Ingress ACLs - actual policy drops (look for `reg0=0x8000`) - **Table 0**: Initial classification drops - **Tables < 64**: Generally meaningful drops ## Common Analysis Scenarios ### 1. Troubleshooting Packet Drops ```bash # Quick analysis (default mode, no ovsdb-tool) python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ ``` Look for: - **ACTIVE DROP FLOWS** section showing flows dropping packets - **PORT STATISTICS** showing ports with drops/errors ### 2. Investigating Pod Connectivity The interface analysis shows pod-to-OVS mapping: - Interfaces with `external_ids` containing `iface-id` - Interface names ending with `_h` (veth host side) ### 4. Datapath Health Check The upcall stats show: ``` DATAPATH FLOW TABLE HEALTH Current flows: 155 / 200,000 (0.1% used) Average: 156, Max seen: 215 ✓ Flow table healthy ``` If usage > 90%, flows are Gallery → Catalog Promotion Pipeline ``` tched_router reads plugin PluginSchema blob ↓ (sealed blob at /dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/..blob) gemma_brain / op-gallery-gen generates Spec ↓ /api/gallery-gen/* (op-web Axum: ui_model.rs) → /dev/shm/ui-specs.json ↓ Gallery page (/gallery) — human reviews ↓ human promotes Catalog page (/catalog) — approved specs only ↓ renders in React dashboard ``` Schema hash pinning (critical — see `.specs/generative-ui-catalog/vision.md`): - Gallery entries MUST carry the `schema_hash` they were drawn against. - Catalog entries are PINNED to that hash. - A reseal identifies which approved elements are stale. - Never promote without verifying hash matches the current sealed blob. - Plugin presence comes from the current sealed manifest; counts change with reseals. --- ## 8. D-Bus json_render Plugin **File:** `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/json_render.rs` Publishes the full json-render surface at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/json_render`: - `packages` — `@json-render/*` package inventory - `components` — catalog component declarations - `actions` — action type declarations - `validation_checks` — built-in validation rules - `directives` — `$format`, `$math`, `$concat`, `$count`, etc. - `methods` — D-Bus method surface - `inspector_fields` — uncapped fields from authoritative packages - `source` — provenance (docs URL, repo URL, commit hash) This blob is what generative runs read to know the available surface area. --- ## 9. spec-builders Utility **File:** `src/json-render/spec-builders.ts` ```typescript import { dataToSpec, streamToSpec } from "@/json-render"; // Any JSON → renderable spec (uses card/kv/container) const spec = dataToSpec(myJsonObject, "My Label"); // List of streaming messages → spec const spec = streamToSpec(messageArray, "Stream Title"); ``` Use when rendering raw gRPC response data without a custom component. --- ## 10. Checklist: Adding a New Feature Page - [ ] Add `NavItem` to `NAV_MANIFEST` in `navigation/manifest.ts` - [ ] Create `src/json-render/pages/.pagespec.ts` with a typed `Spec` - [ ] Register in `pages/index.ts` PAGE_SPECS map (or use legacy React route) - [ ] If new components needed: - [ ] Add to `catalog/catalog.ts` (Zod schema + description) - [ ] Implement in `catalog/components/.tsx` using `El<"name">` type - [ ] Register in `catalog/registry.tsx` - [ ] For factory methods: `client.callSubid({ subid: "factory.", input: {} })` - [ ] For schema hash integrity: verify blob hash before promoting gallery → catalog - [ ] Mark `wip: true` on nav entry until real backend is wired --- ## 11. Key File Locations | What | Path | |---|---| | Catalog contract (reference layout; inspect target first) | `/srv/git/3tched.com/src/json-render/catalog/catalog.ts` | | Component registry | `src/json-render/catalog/registry.tsx` | | Shell components | `src/json-render/catalog/components/shell.tsx` | | Dashboard widgets | `src/json-render/catalog/components/dashboard.tsx` | | Network components | `src/json-render/catalog/components/network.tsx` | | Primitives | `src/json-render/catalog/components/primitives.tsx` | | Nav manifest | `src/json-render/navigation/manifest.ts` | | Page specs index | `src/json-render/pages/index.ts` | | Shell spec | `src/json-render/shell/shellSpec.ts` | | Spec builders | `src/json-render/spec-builders.ts` | | Factory gRPC types | `src/grpc/gen/plugin_methods/factory__*.ts` | | gRPC client | `src/grpc/client.ts` | | json_render plugin | `/srv/git/odbus/crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/json_render.rs` | | schema_renderer plugin | `/srv/git/odbus/crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/schema_renderer.rs` | | tched_router plugin | `/srv/git/odbus/crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/tched_router.rs` | | Gallery/catalog routes | `/srv/git/odbus/crates/op-web/src/handlers/ui_model.rs` | | json-render library | `/srv/git/json-render/packages/core/src/` | | json-render.dev docs | https://json-render.dev/docs | --- name: ovs-db-analysis description: >- Analyze Open vSwitch data from sosreport — conf.db, OpenFlow dumps, port stats, tunnels, and datapath health. Use when troubleshooting OVS packet drops, flow performance, bridge/port/interface issues, DPDK vs kernel datapath, or when the user mentions sosreport openvswitch, ovs-ofctl, ovsdb-tool, or ovs-db-analysis. --- # OVS Database and Flow Analysis This skill provides detailed analysis of Open vSwitch (OVS) data collected via sosreport. It operates in four modes: 1. **Default mode**: Full analysis - conf.db + all text files (requires ovsdb-tool, falls back to text files if not available) 2. **Database mode (`--db`)**: Database only - analyze conf.db (requires ovsdb-tool) 3. **Text files mode (`--flows-only`)**: Text files only - no ovsdb-tool needed 4. **Query mode (`--query`)**: Run custom OVSDB JSON queries (requires ovsdb-tool) ## When to Use This Skill Use this skill when: - **Troubleshooting packet drops** - Find drop flows being hit - **Analyzing flow performance** - View top flows by packet count - Analyzing OVS configuration from a sosreport - Troubleshooting bridge, port, or interface issues - Investigating DPDK vs kernelspace datapath - Reviewing tunnel configurations (VXLAN, Geneve, GRE) - Checking port statistics (drops, errors, traffic) - Mapping Kubernetes pods to OVS interfaces ## Prerequisites **Default mode** (full analysis): - **ovsdb-tool** must be installed (from openvswitch package) - Falls back to `--flows-only` if ovsdb-tool not found - Sosreport with `sos_commands/openvswitch/` directory and `conf.db` **Database mode** (`--db`): - **ovsdb-tool** must be installed (from openvswitch package) - Check: `which ovsdb-tool` - Fedora/RHEL: `sudo dnf install openvswitch` - Ubuntu/Debian: `sudo apt install openvswitch-common` - Sosreport with `conf.db` file **Text files mode** (`--flows-only`): - No special tools needed - works out of the box! - Sosreport with `sos_commands/openvswitch/` directory **Query mode** (`--query`): - **ovsdb-tool** must be installed - Incompatible with `--flows-only` ## File Locations in Sosreport The sosreport collects: ``` sosreport-hostname-date/ ├── etc/openvswitch/conf.db (OVS database - for --db mode) ├── var/lib/openvswitch/conf.db (alternate location) └── sos_commands/openvswitch/ (default mode uses these) ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_show (topology) ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_bridge (bridge details) ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_interface (interface details) ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_Open_vSwitch (system info) ├── ovs-ofctl_dump-flows_ (OpenFlow entries) ├── ovs-ofctl_dump-ports_ (Port statistics) ├── ovs-appctl_coverage.show (internal stats) ├── ovs-appctl_upcall.show (datapath health) ├── ovs-appctl_tnl.ports.show_-v (tunnel ports) └── ... ``` ## Analysis Script The analysis script is located at: ``` /skills/ovs-db-analysis/scripts/analyze_ovs_db.py ``` ## Implementation Steps ### Step 1: Locate the Analysis Script ```bash SCRIPT_PATH=$(find ~ -name "analyze_ovs_db.py" -path "*/sosreport/skills/ovs-db-analysis/scripts/*" 2>/dev/null | head -1) if [ -z "$SCRIPT_PATH" ]; then echo "ERROR: analyze_ovs_db.py script not found." exit 1 fi ``` ### Step 2: Run the Analysis ```bash # Default: Full analysis - conf.db + text files (requires ovsdb-tool) python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport-hostname-date/ # Analyze from archive python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport-hostname-date.tar.xz # Database only mode (requires ovsdb-tool) python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --db # Text files only mode (no ovsdb-tool needed) python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --flows-only ``` ### Step 3: Custom Queries (Optional, requires --db) For specific investigations, use raw OVSDB queries: ```bash # Query all bridges python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Bridge", "where":[], "columns":["name","datapath_type","fail_mode"]}]' # Query VXLAN interfaces python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Interface", "where":[["type","==","vxlan"]], "columns":["name","options"]}]' # Query interfaces with errors python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Interface", "where":[], "columns":["name","error"]}]' ``` ## Analysis Output The default mode analyzes: | Analysis | Source File | Description | |----------|-------------|-------------| | System Info | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_Open_vSwitch` | OVS/DPDK version, system type, external IDs | | Topology | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_show` | Bridge overview with ports grouped by type | | Bridge Details | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_bridge` | Datapath type, fail mode, CT zones | | Interfaces | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_interface` | By type, pod interfaces with mapping | | OpenFlow | `ovs-ofctl_dump-flows_*` | Flow counts, drops, top flows | | Port Stats | `ovs-ofctl_dump-ports_*` | RX/TX drops and errors | | Tunnels | `ovs-appctl_tnl.ports.show_-v` | Configured tunnel ports | | Datapath Health | `ovs-appctl_upcall.show` | Flow table usage vs limit | | OVS Stats | `ovs-appctl_coverage.show` | Internal counters (netlink, OVSDB, etc.) | ## OpenFlow Analysis Features | Feature | Description | |---------|-------------| | Flow Count | Total flows per bridge (total, drop, with hits) | | Drop Detection | Flows with `actions=drop` that have packet hits | | Top Flows | Most active flows sorted by n_packets | | Table Distribution | Flow counts per OpenFlow table | | Port Drops | RX/TX drop counters per port | | Port Errors | RX/TX error counters per port | | Datapath Health | Flow table usage vs limit (from upcall.show) | | OVS Stats | Internal statistics (netlink, OpenFlow, OVSDB transactions) | ## OVN Internal Tables (Ignore Drops in These) When analyzing drop flows in OVN-managed bridges (br-int), **ignore drops in table 44 and tables 64-87** as these are internal OVN mechanics, not security policy or real packet drops. > **⚠️ Note:** OVN and OVS are complex systems and table mappings can change between releases. Always verify drop analysis against the specific OVN version in use. When in doubt, check the OVN source code for your release. | Table | Name | Purpose | |-------|------|---------| | **44** | **CHK_LB_OUTPUT** | **Loopback prevention - drops packets that would loop back (high volume, normal)** | | 64 | SAVE_INPORT | Save ingress port for later | | 65 | LOG_TO_PHY | Logical to physical mapping | | 66 | MAC_BINDING | MAC binding lookups | | 67 | MAC_LOOKUP | MAC address table lookups | | 68-69 | CHK_LB_HAIRPIN | Load balancer hairpin checks | | 70 | CT_SNAT_HAIRPIN | Conntrack SNAT hairpin | | 71-72 | GET/LOOKUP_FDB | FDB (forwarding DB) lookups | | 73-74 | CHK_IN_PORT_SEC | Ingress port security | | 75 | CHK_OUT_PORT_SEC | Egress port security | | 76-77 | ECMP_NH | ECMP next-hop handling | | 78 | CHK_LB_AFFINITY | Load balancer affinity | | **79** | **MAC_CACHE_USE** | **MAC cache miss (high volume, normal)** | | 80 | CT_ZONE_LOOKUP | Conntrack zone lookup | | 81-83 | CT_ORIG_*_LOAD | Conntrack original tuple loading | | 84 | FLOOD_REMOTE_CHASSIS | Remote chassis flooding | | 85 | CT_STATE_SAVE | Conntrack state save | | 86 | CT_ORIG_PROTO_LOAD | Conntrack protocol loading | | 87 | GET_REMOTE_FDB | Remote FDB lookup | **Relevant drop tables for troubleshooting:** - **Table 9**: Ingress ACLs - actual policy drops (look for `reg0=0x8000`) - **Table 0**: Initial classification drops - **Tables < 64**: Generally meaningful drops ## Common Analysis Scenarios ### 1. Troubleshooting Packet Drops ```bash # Quick analysis (default mode, no ovsdb-tool) python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ ``` Look for: - **ACTIVE DROP FLOWS** section showing flows dropping packets - **PORT STATISTICS** showing ports with drops/errors ### 2. Checking DPDK Configuration ```bash # Default mode shows DPDK info from text files python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ # Or use database mode for custom queries python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Open_vSwitch", "where":[], "columns":["dpdk_initialized","other_config"]}]' ``` ### 3. Investigating Pod Connectivity The interface analysis shows pod-to-OVS mapping: - Interfaces with `external_ids` containing `iface-id` - Interface names ending with `_h` (veth host side) ### 4. Datapath Health Check The upcall stats show: ``` DATAPATH FLOW TABLE HEALTH Current flows: 155 / 200,000 (0.1% used) Average: 156, Max seen: 215 ✓ Flow table healthy ``` If usage > 90%, flows are being evicted too aggressively. ## Output Example ``` ================================================================================ OVS ANALYSIS - sosreport-hostname-2024-01-15 ================================================================================ Mode: Text file analysis (no ovsdb-tool required) ================================================================================ OVS SYSTEM INFORMATION ================================================================================ Field Value ------------------------- -------------------------------------------------- OVS Version "3.3.4-62.el9fdp" DB Version "8.5.0" System Type rhcos System Version "4.16" DPDK Initialized false Datapath Types [netdev, system] External IDs: hostname: master2.example.com ovn-encap-ip: 10.32.110.5 ovn-encap-type: geneve ================================================================================ OVS TOPOLOGY ================================================================================ System UUID: 7e9a3f70-86fa-4578-a849-4fd807a64a10 Total Bridges: 2 Bridge: br-ex ports: 3 internal: br-ex patch: patch-br-ex-to-br-int system: nm-bond Bridge: br-int fail_mode: secure datapath_type: system ports: 12 geneve: 9 ports internal: ovn-k8s-mp0, br-int patch: patch-br-int-to-br-ex ================================================================================ OPENFLOW ANALYSIS ================================================================================ Bridge: br-int ---------------------------------------------------------------------- Total flows: 2,017 Flows with hits: 318 Drop flows: 150 (9 actively dropping) ⚠️ ACTIVE DROP FLOWS (9): table=40, priority=0, packets=8,105 table=79, priority=100, packets=1,356 match: ip,reg14=0x2,metadata=0x5,dl_src=00:62:0b:ea:b5:e0 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- DATAPATH FLOW TABLE HEALTH -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Current flows: 155 / 200,000 (0.1% used) Average: 156, Max seen: 215 ✓ Flow table healthy ``` ## Error Handling | Error | Solution | |-------|----------| | `ovsdb-tool not found` | Install openvswitch package OR use default mode (no --db) | | `conf.db not found` | Use default mode (analyzes text files instead) | | `sos_commands/openvswitch not found` | Ensure sosreport has OVS data collected | ## See Also - [OVN Database Analysis](../../must-gather/skills/must-gather-analyzer/scripts/analyze_ovn_dbs.py) - For OVN NB/SB databases - [sosreport openvswitch plugin](https://github.com/sosreport/sos/blob/main/sos/report/plugins/openvswitch.py) - What sosreport collects

# Add Voice

Add Grok Speech to Speech to an existing app. Run on `/add-voice`, typed **Voice Mode**, or clear “add Grok voice” intent.

## Goal

Working duplex path: user-app mic in, audio out, `wss://api.x.ai/v1/realtime?model=grok-voice-latest`, safe auth. Cursor has no native mic; wire the **app** (or a sample client), not the IDE.

## Protocol first

Language-agnostic event loop. **TypeScript samples default.** Short Python twins only where the client API differs (e.g. `ws` vs `websockets`).

## Docs

- https://docs.x.ai/developers/model-capabilities/audio/speech-to-speech
- https://docs.x.ai/developers/model-capabilities/audio/ephemeral-tokens
- Pricing (cite docs only): https://docs.x.ai/developers/pricing (~$0.08/min STS + $0.004/text item; max session 120 min)

## Steps

1. **Map the app**
   - Stack: none, OpenAI Realtime, STT→LLM→TTS cascade, TTS/STT only.
   - Client: web / Node / iOS / Android / server.
   - If a cascade or OpenAI Realtime exists: replace it with the single duplex loop below (URL, model, voice, event diffs); keep standalone `/v1/stt` or `/v1/tts` only if the product still needs one-shot listen or speak outside the agent.

2. **Auth**
   - Server: Bearer `XAI_API_KEY`.
   - Browser/mobile: backend `POST https://api.x.ai/v1/realtime/client_secrets`, client uses ephemeral token (Bearer or browser `sec-websocket-protocol`: `xai-client-secret.<token>`).
   - Never put a long-lived key in client bundles. Do not paste keys in chat.

3. **Connect + session**
   - URL: `wss://api.x.ai/v1/realtime?model=grok-voice-latest`
   - On open: `session.update` with `voice` (default `eve`), `instructions`, `turn_detection: { type: "server_vad" }` (or `null` for push-to-talk), PCM 24 kHz unless the app already standardizes elsewhere.
   - Set `audio.input.transcription.model: "grok-transcribe"` or no user transcript arrives (`conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.updated` is cumulative, not a delta).
   - Tools if needed: `web_search`, `x_search`, `file_search`, `mcp`, custom `function`.

4. **Audio I/O (app-side)**
   - One `AudioContext` per session for capture and playback, created inside the user gesture (autoplay policy). Ask for 24 kHz; if the browser gives another rate, resample before sending.
   - Mic → AudioWorklet in ~100 ms chunks → `input_audio_buffer.append` (or binary transport). Start WS and mic in parallel; buffer early audio, flush on open.
   - Play `response.output_audio.delta` immediately; schedule with a ~150 ms lead so chunks butt together. On `input_audio_buffer.speech_started`, stop everything queued (barge-in).
   - Transcript rows: create the user row on `input_audio_buffer.committed` (`item_id`), fill it on `…transcription.updated`; assistant text from `response.output_audio_transcript.delta` / `.done`, close the turn on `response.done`.
   - On function tools: `function_call_output`, finish playback, then `response.create`.

5. **Composer UI convention**
   - One primary button, right side of the composer. Empty composer → **waveform** icon (stroked, e.g. Phosphor `WaveformIcon weight="bold"`; never the `fill` weight, which renders as a blob at 16 px), starts voice mode. Any text present → classic **send** arrow; in voice mode that text goes into the live session (`conversation.item.create` + `response.create`). Text reply streaming → stop square.
   - While voice is live the same button shows an **animated waveform** (4 bars, ~3 px wide, 2 px gap, ~16 px tall, min scale 0.4 so they stay legible in a 28 px button) and ends the session on click. Phase drives the animation: listening slow, speaking fast, connecting/thinking slower and slightly dimmed (opacity ≥ 0.75). Honor `prefers-reduced-motion`. No X button, no pulsing ring.
   - Status lives **in the composer, not around it**: the placeholder reads `Connecting…` / `Listening…` / `Thinking…` / `Speaking…`, plus an `sr-only` `role="status"`. No separate status row.
   - The **microphone icon is reserved for dictation** (`/add-dictation`). Never use it for voice mode.

6. **TS skeleton (default)**

```ts

// Node: pass Authorization header. Browser: use xai-client-secret.<token> protocol.

ws.addEventListener("open", () => {

    type: "session.update",

      voice: "eve",

      turn_detection: { type: "server_vad" },
    },
  }));
});

ws.addEventListener("message", (ev) => {
  const event = JSON.parse(String(ev.data));
  if (event.type === "response.output_audio.delta") {

  }
});
```

7. **Python twin (only if the app is Python)**

url = "wss://api.x.ai/v1/realtime?model=grok-voice-latest"
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['XAI_API_KEY']}"}

   - Hand the app to the user with **headphones**. On speakers the mic hears the reply and the model answers itself; that is echo, not a bug in the loop.
   - Iterate with `/debug-voice`.

## Out of scope

- Speech-to-text only (`/add-dictation`), speaking text (`/add-read-aloud`)
- Image generation and text-only inference
- Invented endpoints, events, or CLI flags

# Add Dictation

Add Grok Speech to Text to an existing app: a mic button that dictates into the composer, live captions, or transcripts of recorded audio. Run on `/add-dictation`, typed **Dictate**, or clear “transcribe” intent. Cursor has no mic; wire the **app**, not the IDE.

## Docs

- https://docs.x.ai/developers/model-capabilities/audio/speech-to-text
- Model selection (read first): https://docs.x.ai/developers/model-capabilities/audio/speech-to-text#model-selection
- Pricing (cite docs only): https://docs.x.ai/developers/pricing

## Model

Before any STT call, read the model-selection section and pass the **latest listed** model as `model`. Do not invent ids or reuse a stale one from this skill. REST: form field before `file`. Streaming: query param. Official examples currently send `grok-voice-transcribe-2.0`. Listed today: `grok-voice-transcribe-2.0` (best), `grok-voice-transcribe-1.0` (original; API default when `model` is omitted).

## Pick the path

| Need | Path |
| --- | --- |
| Tap, speak, tap, text appears. Uploaded files. URLs. | **Batch** `POST https://api.x.ai/v1/stt` (default) |
| Text appears while speaking: captions, long dictation, push-to-talk | **Streaming** `wss://api.x.ai/v1/stt` through a backend relay |

Batch is the default for a composer mic button: one request, no socket, the key never leaves the server. Go streaming only when the UX needs interim text.

## Auth

- Bearer `XAI_API_KEY`, server side only. The STT docs document no ephemeral-token flow, and browsers cannot set WebSocket headers, so browser streaming goes through your backend relay. Do not invent a token flow.
- Never put the key in a client bundle. Do not paste keys in chat.

## Steps

1. **Map the app**
   - Composer or input component, where the text should land (insert at cursor vs replace), server framework, package manager.
   - The **microphone icon belongs to dictation**. If `/add-voice` is installed, its waveform primary button stays as is; add the mic as a secondary ghost button beside it.
   - Existing mic capture? If `/add-voice` ran, its PCM capture can feed streaming STT; pass its rate as `sample_rate`. 16 kHz is the model’s native rate; other supported rates (8000, 16000, 22050, 24000, 44100, 48000) are resampled server side.

2. **Batch path (default)**
   - Client: `MediaRecorder` → `Blob` → `POST` to your own route. The endpoint auto-detects containers (WAV, MP3, OGG, Opus, FLAC, AAC, MP4, M4A, MKV, WebM), so send whatever `MediaRecorder` produces.
   - Server: forward as `multipart/form-data`. Option fields first, **`file` last**; fields after `file` may be ignored. `file` or `url`, max 500 MB. `model` from docs (latest listed).

```ts
// server (any runtime with fetch + FormData)
export async function transcribe(blob: Blob, filename: string) {
  const form = new FormData();
  form.append("model", "grok-voice-transcribe-2.0"); // latest from docs; re-read model-selection
  form.append("format", "true");     // written-form numbers/currency; requires language
  form.append("language", "en");
  // form.append("keyterm", "Acme"); // repeat per term, ≤100 terms × 50 chars
  form.append("file", blob, filename); // last
  const res = await fetch("https://api.x.ai/v1/stt", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.XAI_API_KEY}` },
    body: form,
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`STT ${res.status}`); // 400 bad input, 413 >500 MB, 429 back off, 502 url fetch failed, 503 retry
  return (await res.json()) as {
    text: string; language: string; duration: number;
    words?: { text: string; start: number; end: number; speaker?: number }[];
    channels?: { index: number; text: string; words: unknown[] }[];
  };
}
```

```ts
// client
const mime = MediaRecorder.isTypeSupported("audio/webm;codecs=opus") ? "audio/webm;codecs=opus" : "audio/mp4";
const rec = new MediaRecorder(stream, { mimeType: mime });
const parts: BlobPart[] = [];
rec.ondataavailable = (e) => parts.push(e.data);
rec.onstop = async () => {
  const fd = new FormData();
  fd.append("file", new Blob(parts, { type: mime }), "dictation");
  const { text } = await (await fetch("/api/dictation", { method: "POST", body: fd })).json();
  insertAtCursor(text);
};
rec.start(); // second tap: rec.stop()
```

3. **Streaming path**
   - Relay: server holds the key, upgrades the browser socket, forwards binary frames and client control messages up, JSON events down. Build the query string server side. `model` from docs (latest listed).

```ts
import { WebSocketServer, WebSocket } from "ws";

new WebSocketServer({ port: 8788 }).on("connection", (client) => {
  const q = new URLSearchParams({ model: "grok-voice-transcribe-2.0", sample_rate: "16000", encoding: "pcm", interim_results: "true", language: "en" });
  const up = new WebSocket(`wss://api.x.ai/v1/stt?${q}`, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.XAI_API_KEY}` } });
  up.on("message", (d) => client.send(d.toString()));                       // transcript.* and error events
  client.on("message", (d, isBinary) => up.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN && up.send(d, { binary: isBinary })); // audio + finalize/audio.done
  const end = () => { client.close(); up.close(); };
  up.on("close", end); up.on("error", end); client.on("close", end);
});
```

   - Browser capture: PCM16 little-endian, mono, 16 kHz, **100 ms frames = 3,200 bytes**, raw binary, no base64. Wait for `transcript.created` before sending. `MediaRecorder` output is a container, not raw frames; do not stream it.

```ts
const ws = new WebSocket(relayUrl); ws.binaryType = "arraybuffer";
const ctx = new AudioContext({ sampleRate: 16000 }); // if ctx.sampleRate !== 16000, downsample in the worklet
await ctx.audioWorklet.addModule("/pcm16-worklet.js"); // Float32 → Int16LE, posts one 3,200-byte frame per 100 ms
const node = new AudioWorkletNode(ctx, "pcm16");
ctx.createMediaStreamSource(stream).connect(node);
let ready = false;
node.port.onmessage = (e) => ready && ws.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN && ws.send(e.data);

let committed = "", locked = "", live = "";
ws.addEventListener("message", (e) => {
  const ev = JSON.parse(e.data);
  if (ev.type === "transcript.created") ready = true;
  else if (ev.type === "transcript.partial") {
    if (ev.speech_final) { committed += ev.text + " "; locked = ""; live = ""; } // complete stitched utterance
    else if (ev.is_final) { locked += ev.text + " "; live = ""; }                // chunk final: text will not change
    else live = ev.text;                                                          // interim: may change
    render(committed + locked + live);
  } else if (ev.type === "transcript.done") ws.close();                          // after audio.done
  else if (ev.type === "error") showError(ev.message);                           // most errors close the socket
});
// stop: ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "audio.done" }))
// push-to-talk release: ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "Finalize" })) then keep streaming (docs show both `finalize` and `Finalize`; the examples use `Finalize`)
```

4. **Options** (query params for streaming, form fields for batch)

| Want | Set |
| --- | --- |
| Latest STT | Read docs #model-selection, pass that `model`. Snapshot: `grok-voice-transcribe-2.0`. Omit → `grok-voice-transcribe-1.0`. Batch: form field. Streaming: query param. |
| Text while speaking | `interim_results=true` |
| “one hundred dollars” → `$100` | streaming: `language=en`; batch: `format=true` + `language=en` |
| Product names, jargon | `keyterm=` repeated |
| Not cut off mid-sentence while dictating numbers | `smart_turn=0.7&smart_turn_timeout=3000` |
| Faster or slower end of utterance | `endpointing=` ms, default 400 |
| Who said what (meetings) | `diarize=true` → `words[].speaker` |
| Agent and customer on separate channels | `multichannel=true&channels=2` (PCM only, not Opus) |
| Keep “um”, “uh” | `filler_words=true` (removed by default) |
| Low bandwidth or mobile | `encoding=opus`, exactly one raw Opus packet per frame, omit `sample_rate` |
| Raw audio to batch | `audio_format=pcm|mulaw|alaw` + `sample_rate` |
| Quiet or telephony audio | lower `vad_threshold` (streaming default 0.08, batch 0.5) |

5. **Python twin (only if the server is Python)**

r = requests.post(
    "https://api.x.ai/v1/stt",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['XAI_API_KEY']}"},
    data=[("model", "grok-voice-transcribe-2.0"), ("format", "true"), ("language", "en")],
    files={"file": ("dictation.webm", blob, "audio/webm")},  # requests sends data fields before files
)

270	```ts
271	// server (any runtime with fetch + FormData)
272	export async function transcribe(blob: Blob, filename: string) {
273	  const form = new FormData();
274	  form.append("model", "grok-voice-transcribe-2.0"); // latest from docs; re-read model-selection
275	  form.append("format", "true");     // written-form numbers/currency; requires language
276	  form.append("language", "en");
277	  // form.append("keyterm", "Acme"); // repeat per term, ≤100 terms × 50 chars
278	  form.append("file", blob, filename); // last
279	  const res = await fetch("https://api.x.ai/v1/stt", {
280	    method: "POST",
281	    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.XAI_API_KEY}` },
282	    body: form,
283	  });
284	  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`STT ${res.status}`); // 400 bad input, 413 >500 MB, 429 back off, 502 url fetch failed, 503 retry
285	  return (await res.json()) as {
286	    text: string; language: string; duration: number;
287	    words?: { text: string; start: number; end: number; speaker?: number }[];
288	    channels?: { index: number; text: string; words: unknown[] }[];
289	  };
290	}
291	```

293	```ts
294	// client
295	const mime = MediaRecorder.isTypeSupported("audio/webm;codecs=opus") ? "audio/webm;codecs=opus" : "audio/mp4";
296	const rec = new MediaRecorder(stream, { mimeType: mime });
297	const parts: BlobPart[] = [];
298	rec.ondataavailable = (e) => parts.push(e.data);
299	rec.onstop = async () => {
300	  const fd = new FormData();
301	  fd.append("file", new Blob(parts, { type: mime }), "dictation");
302	  const { text } = await (await fetch("/api/dictation", { method: "POST", body: fd })).json();
303	  insertAtCursor(text);
304	};
305	rec.start(); // second tap: rec.stop()
306	```
307	
308	3. **Streaming path**
309	   - Relay: server holds the key, upgrades the browser socket, forwards binary frames and client control messages up, JSON events down. Build the query string server side. `model` from docs (latest listed).
310	
311	```ts
312	import { WebSocketServer, WebSocket } from "ws";
313	
314	new WebSocketServer({ port: 8788 }).on("connection", (client) => {
315	  const q = new URLSearchParams({ model: "grok-voice-transcribe-2.0", sample_rate: "16000", encoding: "pcm", interim_results: "true", language: "en" });
316	  const up = new WebSocket(`wss://api.x.ai/v1/stt?${q}`, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.XAI_API_KEY}` } });
317	  up.on("message", (d) => client.send(d.toString()));                       // transcript.* and error events
318	  client.on("message", (d, isBinary) => up.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN && up.send(d, { binary: isBinary })); // audio + finalize/audio.done
319	  const end = () => { client.close(); up.close(); };
320	  up.on("close", end); up.on("error", end); client.on("close", end);
321	});
322	```
323	
324	   - Browser capture: PCM16 little-endian, mono, 16 kHz, **100 ms frames = 3,200 bytes**, raw binary, no base64. Wait for `transcript.created` before sending. `MediaRecorder` output is a container, not raw frames; do not stream it.
325	
326	```ts
327	const ws = new WebSocket(relayUrl); ws.binaryType = "arraybuffer";
328	const ctx = new AudioContext({ sampleRate: 16000 }); // if ctx.sampleRate !== 16000, downsample in the worklet
329	await ctx.audioWorklet.addModule("/pcm16-worklet.js"); // Float32 → Int16LE, posts one 3,200-byte frame per 100 ms
330	const node = new AudioWorkletNode(ctx, "pcm16");
331	ctx.createMediaStreamSource(stream).connect(node);
332	let ready = false;
333	node.port.onmessage = (e) => ready && ws.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN && ws.send(e.data);
334	
335	let committed = "", locked = "", live = "";
336	ws.addEventListener("message", (e) => {
337	  const ev = JSON.parse(e.data);
338	  if (ev.type === "transcript.created") ready = true;
339	  else if (ev.type === "transcript.partial") {
340	    if (ev.speech_final) { committed += ev.text + " "; locked = ""; live = ""; } // complete stitched utterance
341	    else if (ev.is_final) { locked += ev.text + " "; live = ""; }                // chunk final: text will not change
342	    else live = ev.text;                                                          // interim: may change
343	    render(committed + locked + live);
344	  } else if (ev.type === "transcript.done") ws.close();                          // after audio.done
345	  else if (ev.type === "error") showError(ev.message);                           // most errors close the socket
346	});
347	// stop: ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "audio.done" }))
348	// push-to-talk release: ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "Finalize" })) then keep streaming (docs show both `finalize` and `Finalize`; the examples use `Finalize`)
349	```

# Add Voice

Add Grok Speech to Speech to an existing app. Run on `/add-voice`, typed **Voice Mode**, or clear “add Grok voice” intent.

## Goal

Working duplex path: user-app mic in, audio out, `wss://api.x.ai/v1/realtime?model=grok-voice-latest`, safe auth. Cursor has no native mic; wire the **app** (or a sample client), not the IDE.

## Protocol first

Language-agnostic event loop. **TypeScript samples default.** Short Python twins only where the client API differs (e.g. `ws` vs `websockets`).

## Docs

- https://docs.x.ai/developers/model-capabilities/audio/speech-to-speech
- https://docs.x.ai/developers/model-capabilities/audio/ephemeral-tokens
- Pricing (cite docs only): https://docs.x.ai/developers/pricing (~$0.08/min STS + $0.004/text item; max session 120 min)

## Steps

1. **Map the app**
   - Stack: none, OpenAI Realtime, STT→LLM→TTS cascade, TTS/STT only.
   - Client: web / Node / iOS / Android / server.
   - If a cascade or OpenAI Realtime exists: replace it with the single duplex loop below (URL, model, voice, event diffs); keep standalone `/v1/stt` or `/v1/tts` only if the product still needs one-shot listen or speak outside the agent.

2. **Auth**
   - Server: Bearer `XAI_API_KEY`.
   - Browser/mobile: backend `POST https://api.x.ai/v1/realtime/client_secrets`, client uses ephemeral token (Bearer or browser `sec-websocket-protocol`: `xai-client-secret.<token>`).
   - Never put a long-lived key in client bundles. Do not paste keys in chat.

3. **Connect + session**
   - URL: `wss://api.x.ai/v1/realtime?model=grok-voice-latest`
   - On open: `session.update` with `voice` (default `eve`), `instructions`, `turn_detection: { type: "server_vad" }` (or `null` for push-to-talk), PCM 24 kHz unless the app already standardizes elsewhere.
   - Set `audio.input.transcription.model: "grok-transcribe"` or no user transcript arrives (`conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.updated` is cumulative, not a delta).
   - Tools if needed: `web_search`, `x_search`, `file_search`, `mcp`, custom `function`.

4. **Audio I/O (app-side)**
   - One `AudioContext` per session for capture and playback, created inside the user gesture (autoplay policy). Ask for 24 kHz; if the browser gives another rate, resample before sending.
   - Mic → AudioWorklet in ~100 ms chunks → `input_audio_buffer.append` (or binary transport). Start WS and mic in parallel; buffer early audio, flush on open.
   - Play `response.output_audio.delta` immediately; schedule with a ~150 ms lead so chunks butt together. On `input_audio_buffer.speech_started`, stop everything queued (barge-in).
   - Transcript rows: create the user row on `input_audio_buffer.committed` (`item_id`), fill it on `…transcription.updated`; assistant text from `response.output_audio_transcript.delta` / `.done`, close the turn on `response.done`.
   - On function tools: `function_call_output`, finish playback, then `response.create`.

5. **Composer UI convention**
   - One primary button, right side of the composer. Empty composer → **waveform** icon (stroked, e.g. Phosphor `WaveformIcon weight="bold"`; never the `fill` weight, which renders as a blob at 16 px), starts voice mode. Any text present → classic **send** arrow; in voice mode that text goes into the live session (`conversation.item.create` + `response.create`). Text reply streaming → stop square.
   - While voice is live the same button shows an **animated waveform** (4 bars, ~3 px wide, 2 px gap, ~16 px tall, min scale 0.4 so they stay legible in a 28 px button) and ends the session on click. Phase drives the animation: listening slow, speaking fast, connecting/thinking slower and slightly dimmed (opacity ≥ 0.75). Honor `prefers-reduced-motion`. No X button, no pulsing ring.
   - Status lives **in the composer, not around it**: the placeholder reads `Connecting…` / `Listening…` / `Thinking…` / `Speaking…`, plus an `sr-only` `role="status"`. No separate status row.
   - The **microphone icon is reserved for dictation** (`/add-dictation`). Never use it for voice mode.

6. **TS skeleton (default)**

```ts
const url = "wss://api.x.ai/v1/realtime?model=grok-voice-latest";
// Node: pass Authorization header. Browser: use xai-client-secret.<token> protocol.
const ws = new WebSocket(url /* , { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } } */);

ws.addEventListener("open", () => {
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({
    type: "session.update",
    session: {
      voice: "eve",
      instructions: "You are a helpful voice agent.",
      turn_detection: { type: "server_vad" },
    },
  }));
});

ws.addEventListener("message", (ev) => {
  const event = JSON.parse(String(ev.data));
  if (event.type === "response.output_audio.delta") {
    // decode base64 PCM and play
  }
});
```

7. **Python twin (only if the app is Python)**

```python

url = "wss://api.x.ai/v1/realtime?model=grok-voice-latest"
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['XAI_API_KEY']}"}

async with websockets.connect(url, additional_headers=headers) as ws:
    await ws.send(json.dumps({
        "type": "session.update",
        "session": {
            "voice": "eve",
            "instructions": "You are a helpful voice agent.",
            "turn_detection": {"type": "server_vad"},
        },
    }))
    async for raw in ws:
        event = json.loads(raw)
        if event.get("type") == "response.output_audio.delta":
            pass  # decode and play
```

8. **Instrument (before the first human test)**
   - Run `/debug-voice`: it proposes a plan, then installs a dev-only log sink (`POST /api/voice/log` → `.voice-logs/<sessionId>.ndjson`, gitignored), a client logger with audio reduced to byte counts, and the session id in the UI, in the app's own language.
   - The same skill carries the fix loop and the symptom → log signature → fix table.

9. **Smoke**
   - Text turn via `conversation.item.create` + `response.create`; confirm audio or transcript events.
   - Confirm no long-lived key in client (grep the built client bundle for the env name and `client_secrets`).
   - Hand the app to the user with **headphones**. On speakers the mic hears the reply and the model answers itself; that is echo, not a bug in the loop.
   - Iterate with `/debug-voice`.

## Out of scope

- Speech-to-text only (`/add-dictation`), speaking text (`/add-read-aloud`)
- Image generation and text-only inference
- Invented endpoints, events, or CLI flags

# Add Dictation

Add Grok Speech to Text to an existing app: a mic button that dictates into the composer, live captions, or transcripts of recorded audio. Run on `/add-dictation`, typed **Dictate**, or clear “transcribe” intent. Cursor has no mic; wire the **app**, not the IDE.

## Docs

- https://docs.x.ai/developers/model-capabilities/audio/speech-to-text
- Model selection (read first): https://docs.x.ai/developers/model-capabilities/audio/speech-to-text#model-selection
- Pricing (cite docs only): https://docs.x.ai/developers/pricing

## Model

Before any STT call, read the model-selection section and pass the **latest listed** model as `model`. Do not invent ids or reuse a stale one from this skill. REST: form field before `file`. Streaming: query param. Official examples currently send `grok-voice-transcribe-2.0`. Listed today: `grok-voice-transcribe-2.0` (best), `grok-voice-transcribe-1.0` (original; API default when `model` is omitted).

## Pick the path

| Need | Path |
| --- | --- |
| Tap, speak, tap, text appears. Uploaded files. URLs. | **Batch** `POST https://api.x.ai/v1/stt` (default) |
| Text appears while speaking: captions, long dictation, push-to-talk | **Streaming** `wss://api.x.ai/v1/stt` through a backend relay |

Batch is the default for a composer mic button: one request, no socket, the key never leaves the server. Go streaming only when the UX needs interim text.

## Auth

- Bearer `XAI_API_KEY`, server side only. The STT docs document no ephemeral-token flow, and browsers cannot set WebSocket headers, so browser streaming goes through your backend relay. Do not invent a token flow.
- Never put the key in a client bundle. Do not paste keys in chat.

## Steps

1. **Map the app**
   - Composer or input component, where the text should land (insert at cursor vs replace), server framework, package manager.
   - The **microphone icon belongs to dictation**. If `/add-voice` is installed, its waveform primary button stays as is; add the mic as a secondary ghost button beside it.
   - Existing mic capture? If `/add-voice` ran, its PCM capture can feed streaming STT; pass its rate as `sample_rate`. 16 kHz is the model’s native rate; other supported rates (8000, 16000, 22050, 24000, 44100, 48000) are resampled server side.

2. **Batch path (default)**
   - Client: `MediaRecorder` → `Blob` → `POST` to your own route. The endpoint auto-detects containers (WAV, MP3, OGG, Opus, FLAC, AAC, MP4, M4A, MKV, WebM), so send whatever `MediaRecorder` produces.
   - Server: forward as `multipart/form-data`. Option fields first, **`file` last**; fields after `file` may be ignored. `file` or `url`, max 500 MB. `model` from docs (latest listed).

```ts
// server (any runtime with fetch + FormData)
export async function transcribe(blob: Blob, filename: string) {
  const form = new FormData();
  form.append("model", "grok-voice-transcribe-2.0"); // latest from docs; re-read model-selection
  form.append("format", "true");     // written-form numbers/currency; requires language
  form.append("language", "en");
  // form.append("keyterm", "Acme"); // repeat per term, ≤100 terms × 50 chars
  form.append("file", blob, filename); // last
  const res = await fetch("https://api.x.ai/v1/stt", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.XAI_API_KEY}` },
    body: form,
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`STT ${res.status}`); // 400 bad input, 413 >500 MB, 429 back off, 502 url fetch failed, 503 retry
  return (await res.json()) as {
    text: string; language: string; duration: number;
    words?: { text: string; start: number; end: number; speaker?: number }[];
    channels?: { index: number; text: string; words: unknown[] }[];
  };
}
```

```ts
// client
const mime = MediaRecorder.isTypeSupported("audio/webm;codecs=opus") ? "audio/webm;codecs=opus" : "audio/mp4";
const rec = new MediaRecorder(stream, { mimeType: mime });
const parts: BlobPart[] = [];
rec.ondataavailable = (e) => parts.push(e.data);
rec.onstop = async () => {
  const fd = new FormData();
  fd.append("file", new Blob(parts, { type: mime }), "dictation");
  const { text } = await (await fetch("/api/dictation", { method: "POST", body: fd })).json();
  insertAtCursor(text);
};
rec.start(); // second tap: rec.stop()
```

3. **Streaming path**
   - Relay: server holds the key, upgrades the browser socket, forwards binary frames and client control messages up, JSON events down. Build the query string server side. `model` from docs (latest listed).

```ts
import { WebSocketServer, WebSocket } from "ws";

new WebSocketServer({ port: 8788 }).on("connection", (client) => {
  const q = new URLSearchParams({ model: "grok-voice-transcribe-2.0", sample_rate: "16000", encoding: "pcm", interim_results: "true", language: "en" });
  const up = new WebSocket(`wss://api.x.ai/v1/stt?${q}`, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.XAI_API_KEY}` } });
  up.on("message", (d) => client.send(d.toString()));                       // transcript.* and error events
  client.on("message", (d, isBinary) => up.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN && up.send(d, { binary: isBinary })); // audio + finalize/audio.done
  const end = () => { client.close(); up.close(); };
  up.on("close", end); up.on("error", end); client.on("close", end);
});
```

   - Browser capture: PCM16 little-endian, mono, 16 kHz, **100 ms frames = 3,200 bytes**, raw binary, no base64. Wait for `transcript.created` before sending. `MediaRecorder` output is a container, not raw frames; do not stream it.

```ts
const ws = new WebSocket(relayUrl); ws.binaryType = "arraybuffer";
const ctx = new AudioContext({ sampleRate: 16000 }); // if ctx.sampleRate !== 16000, downsample in the worklet
await ctx.audioWorklet.addModule("/pcm16-worklet.js"); // Float32 → Int16LE, posts one 3,200-byte frame per 100 ms
const node = new AudioWorkletNode(ctx, "pcm16");
ctx.createMediaStreamSource(stream).connect(node);
let ready = false;
node.port.onmessage = (e) => ready && ws.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN && ws.send(e.data);

let committed = "", locked = "", live = "";
ws.addEventListener("message", (e) => {
  const ev = JSON.parse(e.data);
  if (ev.type === "transcript.created") ready = true;
  else if (ev.type === "transcript.partial") {
    if (ev.speech_final) { committed += ev.text + " "; locked = ""; live = ""; } // complete stitched utterance
    else if (ev.is_final) { locked += ev.text + " "; live = ""; }                // chunk final: text will not change
    else live = ev.text;                                                          // interim: may change
    render(committed + locked + live);
  } else if (ev.type === "transcript.done") ws.close();                          // after audio.done
  else if (ev.type === "error") showError(ev.message);                           // most errors close the socket
});
// stop: ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "audio.done" }))
// push-to-talk release: ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "Finalize" })) then keep streaming (docs show both `finalize` and `Finalize`; the examples use `Finalize`)
```

4. **Options** (query params for streaming, form fields for batch)

| Want | Set |
| --- | --- |
| Latest STT | Read docs #model-selection, pass that `model`. Snapshot: `grok-voice-transcribe-2.0`. Omit → `grok-voice-transcribe-1.0`. Batch: form field. Streaming: query param. |
| Text while speaking | `interim_results=true` |
| “one hundred dollars” → `$100` | streaming: `language=en`; batch: `format=true` + `language=en` |
| Product names, jargon | `keyterm=` repeated |
| Not cut off mid-sentence while dictating numbers | `smart_turn=0.7&smart_turn_timeout=3000` |
| Faster or slower end of utterance | `endpointing=` ms, default 400 |
| Who said what (meetings) | `diarize=true` → `words[].speaker` |
| Agent and customer on separate channels | `multichannel=true&channels=2` (PCM only, not Opus) |
| Keep “um”, “uh” | `filler_words=true` (removed by default) |
| Low bandwidth or mobile | `encoding=opus`, exactly one raw Opus packet per frame, omit `sample_rate` |
| Raw audio to batch | `audio_format=pcm|mulaw|alaw` + `sample_rate` |
| Quiet or telephony audio | lower `vad_threshold` (streaming default 0.08, batch 0.5) |

5. **Python twin (only if the server is Python)**

```python
import os, requests
r = requests.post(
    "https://api.x.ai/v1/stt",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['XAI_API_KEY']}"},
    data=[("model", "grok-voice-transcribe-2.0"), ("format", "true"), ("language", "en")],
    files={"file": ("dictation.webm", blob, "audio/webm")},  # requests sends data fields before files
)
r.raise_for_status(); text = r.json()["text"]
# streaming: websockets.connect(url, additional_headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"}); await ws.send(pcm_bytes)
```

6. **Smoke**
   - Batch: latest `model` from docs (currently `grok-voice-transcribe-2.0`): `curl -X POST https://api.x.ai/v1/stt -H "Authorization: Bearer $XAI_API_KEY" -F model=grok-voice-transcribe-2.0 -F language=en -F file=@short.wav` → 200 with `text`. Same call with `-F format=true` and no `language` → 400.
   - Streaming: dictate two sentences with a pause between them. Expect interim text, then a final; no duplicated or vanished words at the utterance boundary (if words vanish, the stitched `speech_final` text did not include the chunk finals: append instead of replacing `locked`). `audio.done` → `transcript.done`, socket closes.
   - Search the client bundle for `XAI_API_KEY`; it must not be there.
   - Debug from logs with `/debug-voice`; swap its hook points to `transcript.*` events.

## Out of scope

- Speech that talks back (`/add-voice`), speaking text (`/add-read-aloud`)
- Inventing an STT token flow, endpoints, model ids, or event names not in the docs

content.text:
Agreed, it's both.

**Why it's radical:** it moves where the truth about an identity lives. Right now the host is the hub and the container is a label everything points at. Flipped, the container is the hub. A whole layer of code exists only to find and confirm the identity: the interceptor's lookup-then-mint, the bridge refusing a ledger write until a host row exists, and the provision script working out the session id a second time in shell. That layer goes away, and the four copies of the identity fold into one.

**Why it isn't:** almost nothing on the network moves. The door, TLS, WARP, GRE, decoy minting and the Unix socket all stay put. The building blocks already exist:
- The session id is already the container name.
- The btrfs seed/sprout already works as "shared read-only base plus a writable layer per container".
- 3tchedFS is already built as a shared schema with a copy-on-write workspace on top.
- The session anchor move to the interceptor already put identity handling in one spot, the door on `10.0.0.2:8090`.

So this is mostly deleting the search layer and re-homing what exists. Changes that remove code instead of adding it are usually the right ones.

The real risk sits in one seam: the write path. "A file write is the call" only holds if that write goes through MutationEngine into SHM. The authority question from before lives in the same place. If that seam holds, everything else follows.

That also gives a safe order:
1. **Mount 3tchedFS read-only against live SHM.** This proves the mirror still holds up after a month of changes, and it can't break anything.
2. **Wire one write, say a ledger append, from the filesystem through MutationEngine into SHM.** This is the actual test of the idea.
3. **Only then touch the chatbot container's root and the interceptor.**

content.text:
That's clearer than anything in the Cursor chat. Here's how I understand it:

**Today:** every call arrives from outside, and the host stops it to ask whether the identity exists, whether it's real, whether it's allowed. The identity gets checked on each trip.

**Your model:** the identity lives inside the chatbot, and its activity circulates there. It calls the same RPCs on the same sealed schema, but the caller and the thing being changed are the same identity, in the same place. Nothing is left to verify on those calls, because nobody is asking on someone else's behalf.

Two consequences stand out:

- **No new API.** The schema is still the one source of truth. Only where the calls run and who makes them changes, from external and checked to internal and local.
- **Verification happens once, at the edge.** The decoy mints, WARP and GRE deliver, and the door lets the identity in. After that it's inside. The one other place checking still applies is a call that reaches outside the identity: network, OVS, another plugin's state.

It works like a process and the kernel. A process doesn't ask the kernel to verify each read of its own memory; it only makes a syscall when it touches something that isn't its own.

That also mostly answers the authority question from earlier. The identity is authoritative for its own state, and anything shared is still checked at the boundary. The open part is whether its own state also commits to SHM so the rest of the system can see it, and in what private scope.

content.text:
Yes. Inside the identity, a call becomes a write to a file on its own filesystem, and a query becomes a read. No socket, no call stack, no round trip to the host.

For a write to do an RPC's job, it has to carry what the RPC carried. 3tchedFS already has most of that:

| RPC | File write in 3tchedFS |
|---|---|
| Input checked against the method schema | The FUSE write handler checks it against the sealed schema before it commits |
| Error as `tonic::Status` | Error as an errno on the `write()`, e.g. `EINVAL` when the schema rejects it |
| Mutation commits | The write lands in the sled layer (btrfs, copy-on-write) |
| Ledger event | An append-only file, opened with `O_APPEND` |
| Query | Reading the file returns live state, like `/proc` |

One gap: an RPC returns a typed response, but `write()` only returns a byte count or an error. For methods with real output there are two standard patterns. You can write and then read the same file back. Or, as Plan 9 did (every resource a file), each method gets a `ctl` file you write to and a result file you read. The method's output schema then describes that result file.

One distinction matters here. "Disk write" has to mean a write through the 3tchedFS handler, not raw bytes written to storage underneath. The handler is what makes it a validated call rather than a file edit. The btrfs layer below is only where the result lands.

It stretches in one place. The frontal lobe doesn't keep long-term memory; the hippocampus records episodes. The snowball ledger is the hippocampus role: an append-only record of what happened. | Brain | System |
|---|---|
| Senses | The door and decoy (minting, TLS, WARP) |

| Nerve impulses | 3tchedFS reads and writes |

content.text:
That's the core of it: existence stops being something you check and becomes something that's true by construction.

**Today:** the identity is a record *made of* schema, a row in host Cozo shaped by `identity_sled`. The schema exists whether the row does or not, so the row can be missing, stale or duplicated, and every caller has to ask whether it's there. That's where all the verification code comes from.

**With the filesystem:** the schema is only reachable *through* an identity's mount. If there's no identity, nothing is mounted, and there's no schema surface to call. A call can't happen outside an identity, so there's nothing to verify. The question "is the identity there today?" can't even be asked, because anything asking it is running inside the answer.

This isn't a new principle for the project. It's one the project already runs on, applied to identities. AGENTS.md says "the sealed blob IS the plugin": a plugin exists exactly when its blob is in the catalog, and consumers never check a registry to see whether it exists. Your version: the mounted filesystem IS the identity. The plugin rule has held up, which counts in this idea's favor.

The host side follows the same way. The door still has to send an arrival to the right container, but that's routing, not verification. If the container isn't running, the arrival has nowhere to land, which gives the same answer as "no identity" without any lookup.

I've added this to the memory note.

content.text:
Right. You can only lose something that's separate from you. You don't check you're still you before you think a thought; the identity is what the thinking happens in.

Today's design creates that separation: the identity sits in a host row and the activity happens in the container. Every failure the verification code guards against is a way that gap can go wrong. The row goes missing, goes stale, gets duplicated, or disagrees with the provision shell's copy. The checking only exists because of the gap. Take the gap away and all of that goes with it.

What's left isn't loss but death: if the container is destroyed, the identity goes with it, because they're the same thing. That's a durability question, not a verification one, and you already have the answer in reconstruction from the hashed chain plus state. The snowball ledger in the sled is that chain, and it's what brings an identity back.

Everything else is a consequence of that one change, not a second change:
- **The host lookups and the interceptor mint disappear**, because nothing needs to be found.

So it's one change, and most of what follows is deletion.

The one piece that has to be built is the write path. Today a 3tchedFS write lands in its own workspace and stops there. For a local write to stand in for an RPC, it has to validate, commit and become visible to the rest of the system the way the RPC's mutation did. That's the real work in this, and the proof of concept should aim at it first.

Both are true, and that's what you said at the start: "pretty radical change, but not at the same time."

**Mechanically it's small:** the same schema, the same network, and RPCs become local writes.

**Conceptually it changes everything:**
- **Trust:** it no longer comes from being verified; it comes from existing. Nothing has to prove the identity is there.
- **Direction:** everything flows out from the identity, instead of everything reaching in to find it.
- **The host's role:** it stops being the keeper of identities and becomes the world they act on.
- **Failure:** the whole class of "the identity and its record disagree" errors can't happen anymore. What's left is whether the identity is alive or not.
- **How you reason about the system:** you start from the identity and ask what it touches, instead of starting from a call and asking whose it is.

The best changes usually look like that: a small change to how it's built and a large change to what it means. The code gets smaller because the model got simpler.

content.text:
It's less confusing once you treat the chatbot as an identity, just not a human one. The code already does this: in `session_projection.rs` the control-plane chatbot is its own lifelong session, `chatbot-session`, with its own principal (9 grants against the human's 92). The code also forbids it from ever becoming the ambient identity for a human. OD-63 agent runs already execute under the agent's own sled and grants.

So the model has two kinds of identity with the same shape:

| | Human | Control-plane chatbot |
|---|---|---|
| How it comes to exist | Arrives: decoy mint, WARP, door | Born at provisioning, with no arrival |
| Genesis | Stamped on arrival | Actually a genesis, since the container's creation is its birth |
| Its container | Its self | Its self |
| Local writes | Its own memory and ledger | Its own soul, knowledge, ledger |

What gets confusing is a conversation between them, because that's two identities meeting. Two rules keep it straight:

1. **Nothing crosses sleds by accident.** What the chatbot thinks and learns is a local write to its own sled. What belongs to you stays in yours; the principal-first rule already says that.
2. **Acting on the world is a boundary crossing.** When the chatbot changes host state, or does something *for* you, it leaves its own identity, so that call is still checked.

That leaves one real decision: when the chatbot acts on your behalf, whose authority does it use? Its own 9 grants, as OD-63 runs do today, or authority you hand it for that one action?

It's also a practical first test subject. It doesn't come through the decoy, so the proof of concept isn't blocked by the question AGENTS.md still lists as open, which is how the decoy-minted credential reaches the door. And with only 9 grants, the few calls it makes across its boundary are easy to see.

content.text:
That framing works. For the chatbot, the chat is its voice and the data stream is its eyes. "Who sees what the chat sees" breaks into three parts:

**What the chatbot sees:** its own sled, plus the slice of live SHM state that its own grants let it read (its 9), plus whatever you say to it. Nothing more.

**What you see:** what the chatbot says and renders in the chat, plus your own view of the data stream through your own grants: the doorbell, the live panels. You don't see its raw perception, only what it chooses to show you, the same way you don't see through another person's eyes.

**Everyone else:** nothing. The conversation belongs to the two identities in it.

One rule has to hold for this to be safe: **what the chatbot says to you is bounded by what you're allowed to see, not by what it can see.** Otherwise the chat becomes a way around permissions. Ask the chatbot, get shown something your own grants would refuse. Today the chatbot has fewer grants than you, so that can't happen yet. It becomes real as soon as any agent has more reach than the person it's talking to. The json-render skill already states the rule: a generated component never grants permission, and the server enforces the viewer's scope, including on streamed updates.

That leaves one decision for this model: **whose sled remembers the conversation?** If each identity keeps its own experience, you both hold a copy. That's natural, since you each heard it, but then your words live in the chatbot's sled, outside your principal scope. The alternative is that the conversation lives in your sled and the chatbot keeps only what it learned about the system, not what you said. That's closer to principal-first.

content.text:
So "everyone else sees nothing" isn't the full answer. Accountability is the place where others do see something.

Today, Accountability is one of the chat modes, labelled "Ledger view; memory is read-only". In the new model the ledger lives in your sled; it's your history. Adding a community to that fits the model if the direction holds: **the identity publishes a view of its ledger outward; the community never reaches in.** You choose what's shown, others get a read-only projection, and your sled stays yours. This is the same principal-first rule as projects: sharing is a partition the principal controls, not a hole in the identity boundary.

What makes this work is that the snowball ledger is a hash chain:
- The community can check that the history they're shown hasn't been rewritten, without any access to your sled.
- So verification does come back, but for a different question. Not "does this identity exist", which the model made unnecessary, but "is this history intact". That's the question accountability actually needs answered.

It could go one step further. Accountability partners could countersign entries, like witnesses. Then the record isn't only yours: other identities attest that they saw it at that point in the chain. That's a real community mechanism, and it still doesn't break the boundary, because each signature is a write in the witness's own sled.

Two things to settle when you get there:
1. **Who the community is:** other human identities on this system, members of a project, or something wider.
2. **How much you share:** the whole ledger, or entries you choose to publish.

I've added the community aspect to the memory note.

content.text:
Now it clicks. The UI already has both: the chat frame's mode is `live` or `accountability`. The Accountability reference layout is "Ask about the chatbot's reasoning", plus semantic search, plus an Episodes table of Time, Goal, Outcome and Evidence.

That fits the identity model closely:

- **The live chat is where the chatbot acts.** Its activity circulates inside it as local writes, and nothing checks it call by call.
- **The accountability chat is where it answers for what it did.** You question it, and semantic search pulls the episodes that show what actually happened.

So verification doesn't disappear. It moves from *before* every action to *after*, in the record. Nobody checks you before each thing you do, but you answer for it afterward. That's a better trade than gatekeeping every call, and it's the right match for "no verification inside the identity."

One thing has to be solid for the trial to mean anything: **the defendant can't hold the only copy of the evidence.** If the ledger lives in the chatbot's own sled and its writes there are unchecked, it could in principle rewrite its history and recompute the hash chain. Three fixes, all consistent with the model:

1. **Anchor the chain heads outside the chatbot's sled:** committed to SHM, or countersigned by a witness, which is where the community part comes in. The chatbot can still only append, and any rewrite shows.
2. **Build the semantic index from the committed record,** not from the chatbot's own summaries of what it did.
3. **Keep memory read-only during the trial,** as the mode already says. A witness can't edit the record while testifying.

On screen, the chatbot's answer and the matching episodes should sit side by side, so when its story and its record disagree, you can see it.

content.text:
I think it's right, and I'd do it, carefully.

**Why I think it's right:** the project's own history backs it. SIGNALS has been recording symptoms of the gap between identity and activity for months:
- June 13: "Two identity stores that may not reconcile". Provisioning writes to Cozo, runtime reads the sled.
- OD-24: "reconcile provision script with runtime". Still TODO.
- September: an interceptor that mints genesis on the host, metadata that isn't injected, SID1 re-mints.

Those aren't separate bugs. They're the same gap showing up in different places, and your idea removes the gap instead of patching another instance of it. It's also the rule the project already trusts, "the blob IS the plugin", applied to identities. And it pairs well with Accountability: freedom inside, answer for it afterward.

**What worries me:**
1. **The write path is the whole bet.** If filesystem writes can't commit through MutationEngine into SHM cleanly, it quietly becomes a second source of truth, which is the thing you've ruled out.
2. **There's a new failure mode.** "No identity, no filesystem" also means that if the 3tchedFS daemon crashes, a live identity looks dead. Its existence becomes tied to a userspace process staying up.
3. **The foundation is thin.** 3tchedFS is a month behind, has no commits, has been crash-looping, and only 5 of the 66 plugins have state to mirror.

**How I'd stage it, with a stop condition:**
1. Commit 3tchedFS, and mount it read-only against live SHM. Cheap, and it proves the foundation.
2. Make one real write: a chatbot ledger append, going through MutationEngine into SHM, with the chain head anchored outside the chatbot. That single test proves both the write path and the accountability custody. **If it can't work without duplicating state, stop.** That's the sign it's turning into a second plane.
3. Only then move the chatbot's sled into its container. Humans come after that.
4. Remove the interceptor's host lookup last, and keep the old path running until the new one has held up.

Before any of that, I'd write the design note. This whole idea nearly got lost in the Cursor chat once already. Want me to draft it?

content.text:
Then this makes even more sense. Your interest was sitting there, and 3tchedFS gave it a real job.

You're in good company. The best filesystem ideas have always been the utilitarian ones:

- **procfs and sysfs:** the kernel's state as files you read and write. That's the model you reached for tonight.
- **Plan 9:** took it all the way. The network, windows and processes were all files, and `ctl` files replaced most APIs. Your "disk writes instead of RPC calls" is essentially the Plan 9 view.
- **FUSE made it cheap:** sshfs, rclone and s3fs turned remote things into local paths so every existing tool just worked.

Most FUSE projects stop at *viewing* something as files. This one goes further: the filesystem is the **execution surface** for an identity. Reads report live state, writes are validated calls, and the mount existing is the identity existing. That's about as utilitarian as a filesystem gets.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Vercel Zerolang:

## Overview

Zerolang is an experimental graph-native programming language where the semantic graph is the program database. Zero is an experimental systems language from Vercel Labs, currently at v0.1.2, Apache 2.0 licensed, with source files using the .0 extension.

## Key Design Philosophy

Vercel Zero is a systems language built so AI agents can read errors, repair them, and ship native binaries. It's built around "everything is explicit" — no hidden allocators, no implicit async, no magic global variables — with a built-in agent-first toolchain: structured JSON diagnostics, binary size reports, typed repair metadata.

## How It Works with AI Agents

Zerolang is an experimental graph-native programming language where the semantic graph is the program database. Humans ask for outcomes. Agents query the graph, submit checked edits, and prove the result.

The errors come out as JSON with stable codes. The fixes come out as machine-readable plans.

## Technical Specifications

Zero occupies the same design space as C or Rust: it compiles to native executables, provides explicit memory control, and targets low-level environments. The stated binary target is under 10 KiB. There is no mandatory garbage collector, no hidden allocator, no implicit async, and no magic globals.

You can find the documentation at zerolang.ai and the source code on GitHub at vercel-labs/zerolang.

content.text:
**Plan 9** was the operating system Bell Labs built in the late '80s and '90s, made by the same people who created Unix. It took "everything is a file" all the way: the network, windows and other machines were all files you read and wrote. It also gave **each process its own view of the filesystem**, called per-process namespaces. That's close to what you described tonight, each identity with its own root. Linux mount namespaces, which containers are built on, came from that idea.

**The Vercel language is probably Zero ("zerolang").** Your UI already mentions it: the reference layouts have a "Catalog + Zerolang pattern" card. Zero is an experimental systems language from Vercel Labs, built so AI agents can read, repair and ship native programs. The part that feels FUSE-like: the program is a semantic graph that works like a database. Agents query that graph and submit edits that get checked before they land. That's the same pattern as 3tchedFS: the schema is the database, and every write is validated before it commits.

Vercel is also pushing the filesystem idea directly for agents. They open-sourced **bash-tool**, which lets agents find context by running `find`, `grep` and `jq` over files instead of calling APIs. There's a broader "FUSE is all you need" thread about giving agents access to anything through filesystems.

That matters for your idea. Language models are especially good at working with files and shell tools. If the chatbot's world is 3tchedFS, it can use `cat`, `ls` and `grep` on its own identity and the schema, which are the tools it handles best, instead of a custom RPC surface it has to learn.

In spirit, partly. In practice, no.

**Where they overlap:** Zero and your "the plugin IS the schema" rule chase the same thing: one source of truth that agents can query and change safely. In Zero, the program's semantic graph is the database, so there's nothing separate to keep in sync. That's the ideal your schema rule is aiming at.

2. **Timing.** Zero is v0.1.x, announced in May 2026. Your schema system predates it and runs 36 crates.
3. **Rust-first.** Moving the plugins to a brand-new language would be a rewrite, not a swap.

**What you ended up with is the same pattern pointed at a different target:**
- **Zero:** agents change *programs* through checked edits to a graph.
- **3tchedFS:** identities change *live state* through checked writes to the schema.

3tchedFS already lays it out that way: `/plugins/<plugin>/schema.json` for the contract and `/plugins/<plugin>/operations/<method>/` for each method. Zero's idea is already in your design, applied to runtime instead of source code, and your version sits on a contract that's sealed and hashed.

Now that you know Cozo, the link is clear. Zero's "the semantic graph is the program database" is the same move Cozo makes: data as relations, queried with Datalog, including recursive queries that walk a graph. You already have that engine in the project, and it already has generic `graph_node` and `graph_edge` relations. What isn't in it is the schema. The catalog lives only in the sealed blobs.

Loading the sealed catalog into Cozo as a graph would give you Zero's "query the graph" for your own system:
- **The graph:** plugin → method → field → type, method → required capability, plugin → dependency.
- **Queries become one Datalog line each:** "which methods need this capability", "everything that depends on `identity_sled`, directly or not", "which fields are maps".
- **Tie Accountability episodes into it** and you can ask the trial questions that matter: "what did the chatbot touch, and what depends on that?"

One rule keeps this inside your invariants: **the graph is derived, never authored.** It's built from the sealed blobs, keyed by schema hash, and can be deleted and rebuilt at any time. Nobody writes to it directly. Otherwise it becomes the second schema source AGENTS.md forbids.

That gives you two views of the same sealed schema, each doing a different job:
- **3tchedFS** is how an identity *acts* on the schema.
- **The Cozo graph** is how you *ask questions* about it, and about the record.

content.text:
If "it" means Zero, the Cozo side is the right place for its ideas. I wouldn't bring in the language itself, though: it's a v0.1 systems language and the project is Rust-first. What's worth taking is the three patterns it's built on:

1. **The graph is the database.** Cozo already does this. The schema graph from before is that pattern.
2. **Agents make checked edits.** That's the 3tchedFS write path: validate against the sealed schema, then commit.
3. **Errors come back as structured diagnostics with stable codes and a machine-readable fix plan.** This is the piece you don't have yet, and it fixes a weakness I mentioned earlier. A rejected file write can only return an errno like `EINVAL`, which says nothing about *what* was wrong.

Borrowing the third one would look like this:
- A rejected write returns an errno, and also writes a diagnostic next to it: a stable code, the path of the field that failed, the schema rule it broke, and a suggested fix.
- The diagnostic points at nodes in the Cozo schema graph, so an agent can query the graph to see the rule it broke and what depends on that field.

This fits the chatbot well. When a write it makes gets rejected, it can read a diagnostic, look the rule up in the graph, and retry. That's the loop Zero was built around, running on your schema instead of on source code.

The seeds are safe. Here's why Incus is down:

- **The host rebooted at 11:38.** The seeds partition that `/etc/fstab` mounts by UUID (`753de7a7…`) no longer exists. `sdb2` is now `raccoon-root` (`2dcac52c…`), mounted at `/mnt`.
- **The mounts failed silently.** Because of `nofail`, the seeds mount and both bind mounts were skipped without an error. The pinned seed paths under `/opt/op-dbus/releases/20260924-*/identity/` are empty.
- **So `mount-all` fails, `incusd` exits, and every container stays down.**
- **Both seeds survive** in `/var/lib/opdbus-runtime/identities/seeds/`. `router-core-seed.img` and `core-seed.img` match the pinned sha256 values exactly, and both leaf images are present.

I haven't changed anything.

On "take the Cozo btrfs out of them, just the persistent btrfs device": I want to be sure what "them" means before touching live mounts. My best reading: **Incus shouldn't depend on the seed/leaf rootfs machinery at all. The only identity piece that stays is the persistent btrfs device, the Cozo persist (the `identity-chatbot` and `identity-jeremy` loops), and service containers get nothing.** Is that right, or do you mean removing a persist device from the service containers themselves?

#!/bin/sh

    sv start "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    i=0
    until sv check "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; do
