Use this skill proactively when developers have working traffic to ensure they follow the rules.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-conference-calls: Build multi-party calls using Twilio Conference. Covers warm transfer, cold transfer, coaching (whisper), hold vs mute, participant modes, and supervisor barge. Use this skill for any contact center, support line, or scenario requiring transfers, holds, or multi-party calls.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-content-template-builder: Create, manage, and send message templates using Twilio's Content API. Covers template creation for WhatsApp, SMS, RCS, and MMS; variable usage; WhatsApp Meta approval; and sending templates via ContentSid. Use this skill when building structured messages that require pre-approval or consistent formatting across channels.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-conversation-intelligence: Twilio Conversation Intelligence development guide. Use when building real-time or post-call conversation analysis, language operator pipelines, sentiment analysis, agent assist, cross-channel analytics, or querying aggregated conversation insights (sentiment trends, escalation rates, dashboards).
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-conversation-memory: Store and retrieve conversation context using Twilio Conversation Memory. Covers Memory Store provisioning, profile management, traits, observations, conversation summaries, and semantic Recall. Use this skill to give AI agents or human agents persistent memory of conversations across sessions and channels.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-conversation-orchestrator: Configure automatic conversation capture and routing with Twilio Conversation Orchestrator. Covers Configuration creation, channel capture rules, grouping types, status timeouts, Memory Store linkage, Intelligence linkage, and conversation lifecycle. Use this skill to automatically capture SMS, voice, WhatsApp, RCS, and web chat traffic into unified conversations without manually creating conversations or participants.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-conversations-classic-api: Build multi-channel messaging experiences using Twilio Conversations (classic) API. Covers creating conversations, adding participants (SMS, WhatsApp, chat), sending messages, and handling webhooks. Use this skill to manage persistent multi-party or multi-channel conversations beyond single-message SMS/WhatsApp.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-customer-support-architect: Planning skill for building customer service and support systems. Qualifies the developer's needs across the support ladder (self-service → AI agents → contact center), channel mix, and scale to recommend the right Twilio architecture. Handles both "build me a call center" and "add an IVR to my existing support line."
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-debugging-observability: Debug Twilio integrations and set up production observability. Covers the Console Debugger, Monitor Alerts API, Event Streams for error log streaming, status callback tracking, common error codes, and a systematic debugging workflow. Use this skill whenever a Twilio integration produces errors, messages fail to deliver, calls drop unexpectedly, or you need to set up monitoring for a production deployment.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-email-deliverability-advisor: Deliverability advisor for the Twilio Email API specifically. Use ONLY when the developer explicitly mentions Twilio Email, comms.twilio.com, or a Twilio (non-SendGrid) email program. For all other deliverability questions — including generic ones — use twilio-sendgrid-deliverability-advisor.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-email-send: Use when the caller has Twilio credentials (Account SID + Auth Token or API Key SID + Secret) and needs to send email via comms.twilio.com/v1/Emails. This is Twilio-native email — NOT SendGrid. Do NOT use if the caller has a SendGrid API key (SG.-prefix) — use twilio-sendgrid-email-send instead. Covers single sends, batch sends up to 10,000 recipients, Liquid personalization, operation tracking, and error handling.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-enterprise-knowledge: Add knowledge retrieval (RAG) to AI agents using Twilio Enterprise Knowledge. Covers provisioning Knowledge Bases, uploading sources from web URLs, PDFs, and raw text, and running semantic search to retrieve relevant chunks at runtime. Use this skill to ground agent responses in your organization's actual approved content — FAQs, policies, product docs — rather than hallucinated answers.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-iam-auth-setup: Set up and manage Twilio authentication credentials: Auth Tokens, API keys (Standard, Main, Restricted), Access Tokens for client-side SDKs, and credential rotation. Use this skill as a prerequisite foundation before making any Twilio API calls.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-identity-verification-advisor: Planning skill for identity verification and fraud prevention. Qualifies the developer's needs across authentication method, channel selection, fraud risk level, and user experience to recommend the right Twilio Verify + Lookup architecture. Handles login, signup, password reset, and risk-adaptive verification.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-lookup-phone-intelligence: Look up phone number intelligence via Twilio Lookup v2 API. Covers number validation, line type detection (mobile/landline/VoIP), SIM swap detection, caller name, identity match, and SMS pumping risk scoring. Use this skill to validate numbers or assess fraud risk before sending messages or calls.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-marketing-promotions-advisor: Planning skill for marketing and promotional messaging. Use when a developer is figuring out how to set up or architect a marketing campaign on Twilio — channel selection, compliance readiness, audience size, geography, and delivery tracking. Handles open-ended requests like "how do I set up a WhatsApp marketing campaign" or "what's the best way to run promotional SMS." Skip this skill when the developer already knows what they want and is asking for API specs or implementation details.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-messaging-channel-advisor: Planning skill that helps the developer pick the right Twilio messaging channel — SMS, MMS, RCS, or WhatsApp — for a given use case. Qualifies intent across content type, geography, use case (marketing / notifications / OTP / support), cost model, and brand presence. Use when the developer asks "which channel should I use", "SMS vs RCS vs WhatsApp", mentions a country or region, asks about branded messaging, rich content, or fallback — and proactively when the developer says "send SMS" or "text" but the use case (rich content, international reach, branded experience, marketing campaign, transactional notification) would benefit from a different or multi-channel approach. Also invoke alongside twilio-marketing-promotions-advisor or twilio-notifications-alerts-advisor whenever the developer has not yet confirmed a specific channel.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-messaging-overview: Twilio Messaging channel overview and onboarding guide. Covers all channels (SMS, WhatsApp, RCS, Facebook Messenger), the unified Messages API, channel selection guidance, and the recommended setup sequence from first message to production monitoring. Start here before choosing a specific messaging channel.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-messaging-services: Create and configure Twilio Messaging Services for production messaging. Covers sender pools, geo-match, sticky sender, message scheduling, compliance toolkit, SMS pumping protection, link shortening, and intelligent alerts. Use this skill when setting up production-ready messaging infrastructure.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-messaging-webhooks: Receive and respond to inbound messages and track outbound delivery status via Twilio webhooks — across SMS, MMS, WhatsApp, and RCS. Covers webhook request parameters, replying with TwiML, validating webhook signatures for security, and handling status callbacks. Use this skill whenever an agent needs to handle incoming messages on any channel or track outbound message delivery in real time.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-migrate-messaging-to-verify: Migrate an existing OTP / one-time-passcode flow from the Twilio Programmable Messaging API (self-built: generate code → send SMS → validate) to the Twilio Verify API (managed code generation, delivery, expiry, rate limiting, and Fraud Guard). Covers what Verify replaces, creating a Verify Service, replacing send + check logic, E.164 formatting with Lookup, bring-your-own custom codes, error-code translation, and a safe incremental cutover. Use when a developer is moving OTP/2FA delivery off Programmable Messaging onto Verify, or asks "should I use Verify instead of sending my own SMS codes?".
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-notifications-alerts-advisor: Planning skill for transactional notifications, alerts, and reminders. Qualifies the developer's needs across urgency, channel selection, delivery confirmation, and fallback patterns to recommend the right Twilio notification architecture. Handles both "send shipping updates to customers" and "build a multi-channel alert system with delivery confirmation and fallback."
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-numbers-senders: Choose the right Twilio number type and sender BEFORE building. Covers phone numbers (local, toll-free, short code, mobile), alphanumeric sender IDs, WhatsApp senders, RCS agents, international availability, and regulatory bundles. Each number type has its own compliance program — choosing wrong means rebuilding. Use this skill first.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-organizations-setup: Set up and manage Twilio Organizations for centralized account and user governance. Covers the Organization > Account > Subaccount hierarchy, roles (Owner/Admin/Standard), managed vs independent accounts, domain registration, SSO enforcement, SCIM provisioning, and Organization merging. Use this skill when managing multiple Twilio accounts or users across teams.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-rcs-messaging: Send RCS Business Messages via Twilio. Covers compliance onboarding (7-part US process), sender profile setup, sending rich cards and carousels, SMS fallback, device support (Android + iOS 18 caveats), and common errors. Use this skill when building RCS messaging or onboarding an RCS sender.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-regulatory-compliance-bundles: Manage regulatory compliance for international phone numbers. Covers what bundles are, which countries require them, how to create End-Users and Supporting Documents, evaluate and submit bundles, fix evaluation failures, update bundles when regulations change, and ISV multi-account patterns. Use this skill when provisioning numbers outside the US.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-reliability-patterns: Handle rate limits, retries, and failures when building on Twilio at scale. Covers 429 exponential backoff with jitter, per-number throughput limits, StatusCallback resilience, thin-receiver pattern, and fallback chains. Use this skill whenever sending messages or making calls at volume, or when building production-grade Twilio integrations.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-security-api-auth: Choose the right Twilio authentication method and implement it correctly. Covers Auth Token (testing only), API Keys (production standard), OAuth2 client_credentials (time-limited bearer tokens), Access Tokens (client-side SDKs), and test credentials. Use this skill before making any Twilio API calls in production.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-security-compliance-hipaa: Configure Twilio accounts for HIPAA compliance. Covers BAA requirements, HIPAA Project designation (self-service and support), eligible services list, per-product requirements (Voice, SMS, ConversationRelay, Conversation Intelligence, Flex, Verify), message redaction, and what is NOT eligible. Use this skill when developers are building healthcare workflows on Twilio.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-security-hardening: Secure Twilio applications against common attacks. Covers credential management (API keys vs auth tokens), request validation (webhook signature verification), PCI DSS compliance, HIPAA account requirements, SMS pumping prevention, geo-permissions, and account isolation patterns. Use this skill when developers are building or deploying Twilio apps.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-send-message: Send messages via Twilio's Programmable Messaging API across all channels — SMS, MMS, RCS, and WhatsApp. Covers text messages, media, rich content (cards, carousels, buttons), template-based sends, Messaging Services, status callbacks, and WhatsApp's 24-hour service window. - twilio-developer-kit:twilio-sms-isv-setup: Best practices for ISVs (Independent Software Vendors) building SMS features into multi-tenant SaaS platforms using Twilio. Covers customer onboarding for A2P and toll-free compliance, subaccount architecture, sender management, billing patterns, and common ISV pitfalls. Use this when building SMS capabilities that your customers will use to message their end users.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-sms-send-message: SMS and MMS deep-dive reference. For sending SMS, use twilio-send-message instead. Use this skill only when debugging SMS delivery issues or needing SMS-specific details not in the consolidated send skill.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-studio-flows: Build and deploy Twilio Studio flows — visual IVR, SMS/WhatsApp, and conversation automation — by authoring the flow definition JSON and managing it through the Studio REST API. Covers the flow envelope, widgets, transitions, Liquid templating, the draft/published lifecycle, and when to use Studio vs. custom TwiML/code. Use this skill to create, validate, deploy, or update a Studio flow programmatically.

- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-voice-conversation-relay: Build AI-powered voice agents using Twilio ConversationRelay. Handles real-time speech recognition (ASR), text-to-speech (TTS), and bidirectional audio streaming via WebSocket. Covers TwiML setup, WebSocket message types, LLM integration, streaming responses, and voice provider configuration. Use this skill to build voice bots, IVR replacements, or real-time AI voice assistants on Twilio calls.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-voice-outbound-calls: Make outbound phone calls via Twilio's Programmable Voice REST API. Use this skill for outbound calls, sales dialers, or when asking what voice APIs are available.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-voice-twiml: Build voice call logic using TwiML (Twilio Markup Language). Use this skill to define call behavior for inbound or outbound calls.

Use this skill whenever an agent needs to receive HTTP callbacks from Twilio for any product -- messaging, voice, verify, or event streams.
- twilio-developer-kit:twilio-whatsapp-manage-senders: Create, configure, and manage WhatsApp Business senders via Twilio's Channels Senders API. #!/bin/sh
# op-identity-root.sh — bring identities up from their own devices (OD-86).
#
# The device IS the identity. There is no per-identity descriptor: an identity
# exists when /var/lib/opdbus-runtime/identities/<session>/identity.img holds
# a btrfs filesystem labelled identity-<session>. For each one this script
#
#   1) attaches and mounts the device at <identity>/device,
#   2) mounts the container root as overlay(Raccoon, device/upper),
#   3) mounts the identity's lungs (3tchedFS with a call file per method),
#   4) starts the Incus container named <session>.
#
# The shared lower layer is the read-only Raccoon partition, shown through an
# idmapped view so Incus never shifts (chowns) the root into the upper layer.
# A failure stays inside that identity: the script logs it and moves on, and
# it never gates incusd or any service container.
#
# Usage:
#   sudo ./op-identity-root.sh up [<session>...]     # default: every identity
#   sudo ./op-identity-root.sh down <session>...
#   sudo ./op-identity-root.sh status
#
# Environment overrides (defaults shown):
#   RACCOON_UUID=2dcac52c-fb0b-418a-95a4-cb6eacc80209
#   SEEDS=/var/lib/opdbus-seeds            read-only Raccoon mount (fstab)
#   SEEDS_IDMAP=/var/lib/opdbus-seeds-idmap
#   IDMAP='b:0:1000000:1000000000'         must match the containers' idmap
#   IDENTITIES=/var/lib/opdbus-runtime/identities
#   POOL=identity-roots                    Incus dir pool for identity roots
#   LUNGS_RUN=/run/opdbus-lungs
#   THREETCHED_FS=/usr/local/sbin/threetched-fs
set -u

RACCOON_UUID=${RACCOON_UUID:-2dcac52c-fb0b-418a-95a4-cb6eacc80209}
SEEDS=${SEEDS:-/var/lib/opdbus-seeds}
SEEDS_IDMAP=${SEEDS_IDMAP:-/var/lib/opdbus-seeds-idmap}
IDMAP=${IDMAP:-b:0:1000000:1000000000}
IDENTITIES=${IDENTITIES:-/var/lib/opdbus-runtime/identities}
POOL=${POOL:-identity-roots}
POOL_PATH=/var/lib/incus/storage-pools/$POOL/containers
LUNGS_RUN=${LUNGS_RUN:-/run/opdbus-lungs}
THREETCHED_FS=${THREETCHED_FS:-/usr/local/sbin/threetched-fs}
STATE=/dev/shm/opdbus/state
CATALOG=/dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs

log() { printf '%s\n' "op-identity-root: $*" >&2; }

# Session ids are container names; accept only the canonical UUID shape so a
# directory name can never smuggle a path or an option into a command.
valid_session() {
    printf '%s' "$1" | grep -Eq '^[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}$'
}

ensure_lower() {
    if ! mountpoint -q "$SEEDS"; then
        install -d -m 0755 "$SEEDS"
        mount -o ro,noatime "UUID=$RACCOON_UUID" "$SEEDS" || return 1
    fi
    if ! mountpoint -q "$SEEDS_IDMAP"; then
        install -d -m 0755 "$SEEDS_IDMAP"
        mount --bind -o "ro,X-mount.idmap=$IDMAP" "$SEEDS" "$SEEDS_IDMAP" || return 1
    fi
}

loop_for() {
    losetup -j "$1" -O NAME -n 2>/dev/null | head -n 1
}

mount_device() {
    session=$1
    dir=$IDENTITIES/$session
    image=$dir/identity.img
    [ -f "$image" ] || { log "$session: no identity device"; return 1; }
    mountpoint -q "$dir/device" && return 0
    loop=$(loop_for "$image")
    [ -n "$loop" ] || loop=$(losetup -f --show "$image") || return 1
    label=$(blkid -s LABEL -o value "$loop" 2>/dev/null)
    if [ "$label" != "identity-$session" ]; then
        log "$session: device label '$label' does not name this identity"
        losetup -d "$loop" 2>/dev/null
        return 1
    fi
    install -d -m 0700 "$dir/device"
    mount -o noatime "$loop" "$dir/device"
}

mount_root() {
    session=$1
    dir=$IDENTITIES/$session/device
    root=$POOL_PATH/$session/rootfs
    [ -d "$root" ] || { log "$session: no Incus instance on pool $POOL"; return 1; }
    mountpoint -q "$root" && return 0
    mount -t overlay overlay \
        -o "lowerdir=$SEEDS_IDMAP,upperdir=$dir/upper,workdir=$dir/work" "$root"
}

mount_lungs() {
    session=$1
    lungs=$LUNGS_RUN/$session
    mountpoint -q "$lungs" && return 0
    install -d -m 0700 "$LUNGS_RUN"
    install -d -m 0755 "$lungs"
    store=$LUNGS_RUN/.store-$session
    "$THREETCHED_FS" --store "$store" capture \
        --catalog "$CATALOG" --state "$STATE" >/dev/null || return 1
    setsid "$THREETCHED_FS" --store "$store" mount \
        --allow-other --auto-unmount --state "$STATE" \
        --lungs-credential "$IDENTITIES/$session/device/credential/sid1" \
        "$lungs" </dev/null >"$LUNGS_RUN/$session.log" 2>&1 &
    i=0
    until mountpoint -q "$lungs"; do
        i=$((i + 1))
        [ "$i" -ge 20 ] && { log "$session: lungs did not mount"; return 1; }
        sleep 0.5
    done
}

up_one() {
    session=$1
    valid_session "$session" || { log "skipping '$session': not a session id"; return 1; }
    mount_device "$session" || { log "$session: device failed"; return 1; }
    mount_root "$session" || { log "$session: root overlay failed"; return 1; }
    mount_lungs "$session" || log "$session: lungs failed; identity starts without them"
    if incus list "$session" -c s -f csv 2>/dev/null | grep -q '^RUNNING$'; then
        return 0
    fi
    incus start "$session"
}

down_one() {
    session=$1
    valid_session "$session" || return 1
    incus stop "$session" 2>/dev/null
    mountpoint -q "$LUNGS_RUN/$session" && umount "$LUNGS_RUN/$session"
    root=$POOL_PATH/$session/rootfs
    mountpoint -q "$root" && umount "$root"
    dev=$IDENTITIES/$session/device
    if mountpoint -q "$dev"; then
        loop=$(findmnt -n -o SOURCE "$dev")
        umount "$dev" && [ -n "$loop" ] && losetup -d "$loop"
    fi
}

all_sessions() {
    for image in "$IDENTITIES"/*/identity.img; do
        [ -f "$image" ] || continue
        basename "$(dirname "$image")"
    done
}

status() {
    for session in $(all_sessions); do
        printf '%s device=%s root=%s lungs=%s ct=%s\n' "$session" \
            "$(mountpoint -q "$IDENTITIES/$session/device" && echo up || echo down)" \
            "$(mountpoint -q "$POOL_PATH/$session/rootfs" && echo up || echo down)" \
            "$(mountpoint -q "$LUNGS_RUN/$session" && echo up || echo down)" \
            "$(incus list "$session" -c s -f csv 2>/dev/null || echo absent)"
    done
}

command=${1:-status}
[ "$#" -gt 0 ] && shift
case $command in
up)
    ensure_lower || { log "Raccoon lower layer unavailable"; exit 1; }
    [ "$#" -gt 0 ] || set -- $(all_sessions)
    failed=0
    for session in "$@"; do
        up_one "$session" || failed=$((failed + 1))
    done
    [ "$failed" -eq 0 ] || log "$failed identity(ies) did not come up"
    exit 0
    ;;
down)
    [ "$#" -gt 0 ] || { log "name the session(s) to stop"; exit 2; }
    for session in "$@"; do down_one "$session"; done
    ;;
status) status ;;
*)
    log "usage: $0 up [<session>...] | down <session>... | status"
    exit 2
    ;;
esac

| OD-81 | **Complete the human identity seeded Btrfs leaf through canonical provisioning.** | Codex | DONE | Sep 24 complete: received read-only release 20260924-identity-seed activated; canonical own-root repair returned identity-committed/root_and_persist_moved. Existing SID1, genesis, Cozo key and old fstorage bytes preserved; new seeded Btrfs root and private persist binding verified, container remains stopped. Human write/root-repair grants active (88→90), chatbot9 unchanged; write admission proved with duplicate guard. Four private canonical cases and exact helper cold remount/privacy pass. Cozo remains shared device registry, no per-human database copy. First activation rolled back on legacy fwd-443 parent chmod1777; host/source script corrected to0755 without network restart, retry passed. Durable evidence: /opt/op-dbus/recovery/identity-seed-20260924/activation-evidence/DEPLOYMENT.md. |

-| OD-86 | **Identity-centric containers: the container IS the identity, and its calls become local writes.** Invert the design so everything extends from the identity. Today the host keeps the identity (Cozo rows, `identity.json`, the interceptor lookup and mint) and the container is a label. The identity's activity should circulate inside its container, and its RPCs on the same sealed schema become local 3tchedFS writes. No identity means no mount and no schema surface, so nothing checks for existence. | `owner` + `Claude` | WIP | **Sep 26 one-shot (Claude) landed live:** Raccoon (`sdb2`, UUID `2dcac52c…`) mounted ro at `/var/lib/opdbus-seeds`, plus an idmapped ro view at `/var/lib/opdbus-seeds-idmap`. Incus `dir` pool `identity-roots` holds the overlay roots. Identity `414fbc56…` (session kept, genesis unchanged) now runs on device `identity.img`, labelled `identity-<session>`, which holds `upper/`, `work/`, `cozo/` and a root-only `credential/`. Its container runs on overlay(Raccoon idmapped, device/upper) with no Incus shifting and an 8.8 MB upper. Its organ is 3tchedFS `0b0e622`, all 66 plugins, mounted at `/run/opdbus-organ/<session>` and bound at `/opt/run-mounts/3tched`. **Proven:** a btrfs seed cannot back two mounted sprouts at once (kernel 7.2), so the design uses overlay. Incus copies an overlay root into upper unless the lower layer is idmapped and `volatile.last_state.idmap` is preset. From inside the identity, organ reads are live SHM, and `call` writes validate against the sealed schema. **Blocked:** a valid call stops at the `credential` stage because no SID1 has been delivered to the device. **Owner correction (Sep 26):** the session credential is server-side, anchored by the interceptor, and the GUI carries only OIA1. Do not put SID1 on disk. The organ inherits the anchor: 3tchedFS hands each call to the bridge over that identity's own socket, and the bridge dispatches with the sled's SID1. Delivering it is an owner decision tied to the open decoy-credential path. The bridge seam would be after `refresh_credential_owned` commits (`identity_sled_dispatch.rs`), writing that session's SID1 wire to `device/credential/sid1`. **Not built:** the door as organ, meaning a `grpc_server.rs` `call_method` branch that writes arrivals to `/run/opdbus-organ/<session>/…/call` (needs a bridge release). **Manual, not reboot-safe:** these mounts are run by `deploy/scripts/op-identity-root.sh up`, which is not wired to runit. `threetched-fs` sv is down, the POC binary runs from `target/release`, and fstab still names the old seeds UUID. Old storage is archived: boot descriptors are in `/etc/op-dbus/identity-storage.archived-20260926/`, and the instance was renamed `414fbc56-archived-20260926` in the DB only (the leaf dir still carries the old name). Sep 26 owner idea, worked out with Grok in Cursor (transcripts `43a74719…`, `7056f4bf…`). Only the idea exists. **Unchanged:** decoy mint, TLS, WARP, GRE, the `10.0.0.2:8090` door on the host, Unix-socket networking, and the sealed schema. **Changes:** the sled (identity, soul, namespaces, snowball ledger, keys) becomes the writable upper overlay of the container root, over the shared Raccoon seed (→ OD-85). 3tchedFS reads report live state and its writes execute calls after schema validation, like procfs. The interceptor host lookup is removed last. The control-plane chatbot is a non-human identity and the first test subject. The Accountability chat puts it on trial through semantic search over its episodes, with a community aspect. **Stages:** 1) commit `/srv/git/3tchedFS` (no commits yet; `map`/`json_schema` decoder fix is uncommitted) and mount it read-only against live SHM; 2) run one chatbot ledger append as a FS write through MutationEngine into SHM, with the chain head anchored outside the chatbot's sled. **Stop if** that write cannot commit without duplicating state, because that would create a second plane; 3) move the chatbot's sled into its container; 4) humans, then remove the interceptor lookup. **Open questions:** does the identity's own state also commit to SHM, and in what private scope? Whose sled records a conversation? Whose authority does the chatbot use when it acts for a human? **Risk:** a 3tchedFS daemon crash makes a live identity look absent. Rollback set `20260926T052648Z` (`/.snapshot/*-pre-3tchedfs`, chatbot, seed and loop snapshots). **Sep 27:** a full `op-identity-root.sh down`/`up` cycle rebuilt device, root, organ and container from scratch. After 3tchedFS `ff6e84c` caching, organ reads take about 172 µs host-side, compared with 265 µs over HTTP to op-web and a 29 µs raw SHM floor. |

content.text:
I'd bring it in-house, into the odbus-verified workspace as its own crate. The strongest reason is that 3tchedFS keeps **its own private copy of the schema model**: its own `OPBLOB01` blob parser (`source.rs`) and its own `PluginSchema` and `FieldType` (`model.rs`). That duplicate copy is what broke it for a month. The real schema gained `json_schema` and `map`, and 3tchedFS didn't know, so its captures failed on every run. Your rule is one source of truth for the schema. Inside the workspace, 3tchedFS can use the real types from `op-blob` and `op-state-store` directly, and that kind of drift can't happen again.

It also helps with the next steps:
- **Releases:** it would ship through the golden snapshot like the other binaries, which fixes the "old August binary is what's installed" problem from OD-86.
- **The lungs socket:** that work touches 3tchedFS and the bridge at once, which is easier in one repo.
- **Checks:** it would run under the same `/verify` gates as everything else.

It fits cleanly:
- **Dependencies match:** the same `zbus` 5, `jsonschema` 0.29 and `tokio`. Only `fuser` is new.
- **Edition:** it uses Rust 2024 and the workspace uses 2021, but one crate can keep its own edition.
- **License:** the crate is MIT and the workspace is Apache-2.0. Both are permissive, and you own the code, so you can pick either.

How I'd do it:
1. **Import it with its history** using `git subtree`, as `crates/threetched-fs`. Its 5 commits come along.
2. **Add it to the workspace,** have the Haiku worker check and test it, and update the crate count in AGENTS.md.
3. **Swap its private schema copy for the workspace types,** as a separate commit, since that's the actual fix.

`/srv/git/3tchedFS` would then stay only as an archive. Go ahead?

content.text:
There's no technical reason. It was inherited and never revisited:
- **No toolchain pin** holds it back. There's no `rust-toolchain` file, and the host runs Rust 1.97.1, which fully supports 2024.
- **The edition came in with the code.** `/srv/git/odbus` starts on 2026-03-24 with an "initial standalone import" that already said `edition = "2021"`, carried over from `operation-dbus-proto`. This repo was split from that on 2026-09-14 with the same setting.
- **Why 2021 in the first place:** Rust 2024 shipped in February 2025, about 19 months ago. Most `Cargo.toml` files AI assistants write still default to 2021, because that's what most of the examples they learned from use. Once the first crate said 2021, every new crate copied it.
- **Even the setting is split:** 26 crates inherit the workspace edition, but 10 hard-code `"2021"` in their own manifests.

So nobody decided against 2024. It just never came up.

Upgrading is worth it, and it's mostly mechanical:
1. Move the workspace to `edition = "2024"`, and switch the 10 hard-coded crates to inherit it.
2. Run `cargo fix --edition` to rewrite what changes. The main items: temporaries in `if let` and at the end of blocks are dropped at different times, return types capture lifetimes differently, `std::env::set_var` becomes `unsafe`, `unsafe extern` blocks, and `gen` becomes reserved.
3. Run the full `/verify` (fmt, clippy with warnings as errors, all tests) and review the diff. The drop-timing changes are the one place behavior can quietly change, for example a lock held a little longer or shorter.

That's workspace-wide cargo, so under your rule it waits for you to say "workspace." I'd do it right after the 3tchedFS schema swap lands, as its own commit. Want me to go ahead then?

Done. `threetched-fs` now reads as plain `down`, no longer "normally up", so it stays off at boot and won't crash-loop. To undo it: `sudo rm /etc/runit/sv/threetched-fs/down`.

A reboot would still cause trouble in three places:

2. **The chatbot container has autostart off,** and nothing starts it at boot. After the last reboot I started it by hand, and without it the bridge has no identity to work with.
3. **`/etc/fstab` still names the old seeds partition UUID.** Its `nofail` lines fail silently, so it's harmless but misleading. The Raccoon mount is handled by the script instead.

For 1 and 2 the proper fix goes through a release: add an `identity-roots` runit service in `deploy/runit/`, and stage the new `threetched-fs` binary in golden. I can prepare all of that in source now.         "$MONGODB_MCP_ARTIFACT_PATH" "$MONGODB_MCP_SHA256" \
        node_modules/mongodb-mcp-server/dist/esm/index.js
    run mkdir -p \
        "$GOLDEN_DIR/var/log/runit/mongodb-mcp-server"
    ok "staged pinned nlm CLI and MongoDB MCP provider into golden/opt"

    # Runit service definitions tracked in the repo. Explicit retirement is
    # subtractive so a reused golden subvolume cannot resurrect an old unit.
    if [ -f "$RETIRED_SERVICES_FILE" ]; then
        grep -Ev '^[[:space:]]*(#|$)' "$RETIRED_SERVICES_FILE" | while IFS= read -r svc; do
            [ -n "$svc" ] || continue
            [ ! -e "$GOLDEN_DIR/sv/$svc" ] || run rm -r -- "$GOLDEN_DIR/sv/$svc"
        done
    fi
    for svc_dir in "$SCRIPT_DIR"/*/; do
        [ -f "${svc_dir}run" ] || continue
        svc=$(basename "$svc_dir")
        is_retired_service "$svc" && continue
        run mkdir -p "$GOLDEN_DIR/sv/$svc"
        run install -Dm755 "${svc_dir}run" "$GOLDEN_DIR/sv/$svc/run"
        [ -f "${svc_dir}log/run" ] &&
            run install -Dm755 "${svc_dir}log/run" "$GOLDEN_DIR/sv/$svc/log/run"
        [ -f "${svc_dir}finish" ] &&
            run install -Dm755 "${svc_dir}finish" "$GOLDEN_DIR/sv/$svc/finish"
        [ -f "${svc_dir}check" ] &&
            run install -Dm755 "${svc_dir}check" "$GOLDEN_DIR/sv/$svc/check"
    done
    ok "staged runit service definitions into golden/sv"

    # Config the target needs alongside the binaries.
    [ -f "$SCRIPT_DIR/../environment.default" ] &&

the existing received filesystems without exceeding five subvolumes.

## Activate

First migration creates per-file links from established host paths into
`/opt/op-dbus/current`. Preserve every replaced file, directory or symlink
and record its destination in the recovery receipt. Move originals rather
than copying new binaries into the live installation. Create replacement
links under temporary names in each destination directory, then rename
them into place.

| Received path | Host path |
|---|---|
| `bin/<name>` | `/usr/local/bin/<name>` for the explicit release binary inventory and `nlm` |
| `usr/bin/zeroclaw` | `/usr/bin/zeroclaw` |
| `usr/share/op-dbus/{native,ui}-manifests/<file>` | Same absolute host path |
| `libexec/3tched/<helper>` | `/usr/local/libexec/3tched/<helper>` for activated service dependencies |
| `sv/<service>/{run,check,finish,log/run}` | Corresponding files in `/etc/runit/sv/<service>` |
| `etc/opdbus/{capability-grants,mcp-audience-policy,mcp-toolsets}.json` | Corresponding protected policy files in `/etc/opdbus` |
| `etc/op-dbus/zeroclaw-runtime.toml` and skill bundle | Corresponding bootstrap files in `/etc/op-dbus` |
| `etc/emqx/{emqx.conf,base.hocon,acl.conf}` | Corresponding files in `/etc/emqx` |
| `usr/local/share/op-dbus/dashboard/{index.html,assets}` | Same host paths; preserve other dashboard mounts |
| `opt/emqx` and pinned provider installations | Explicit matching host provider paths |

Keep runit service directories and their `supervise/` and log-supervision
state writable. Never symlink the whole service directory into a read-only
release. Keep `/etc/op-dbus` and `/etc/emqx` writable: secrets, issued TLS
files, native gateway pairing state and runtime configuration are not
overwritten by a directory-level switch. Keep identity, Cozo, Qdrant,
Snowball, replay and broker data in their existing durable locations.

Once links and prerequisites are ready, stop the affected application services
before changing the binary/catalog pair. For this bridge/identity release:

```sh
sudo sv down emqx op-web op-grpc-bridge opdbus-grants
sudo ln -s "releases/$release_id" /opt/op-dbus/.current-next
sudo mv -Tf /opt/op-dbus/.current-next /opt/op-dbus/current
```

Activate the received persisted catalog with `opblob persist <received
catalog> /var/lib/opdbus/plugin-blobs`, then `opblob stage-shm`. Startup
consumes that catalog and must never reseal or restore old private SHM state.
Bring up `opdbus-grants` and the bridge before EMQX and op-web, checking their
readiness with `sudo sv check`. Deliberately restart only changed services:
the native router when its configuration changes, grants materialization,
the bridge, EMQX, and op-web. Preserve existing runlevel symlinks, adding only
the explicitly enabled application service when absent. Do not restart or
activate staged network, OVS, uplink, DHCP, session-bus, Xray or container
definitions as an incidental part of application activation.

Check that running executable digests match the received release, live and
persisted catalog manifests match, authenticated MCP works, and the UI
receives its own EMQX wake before reading private committed knowledge.
Report any remaining backend-data failure separately from deployment.

#!/bin/sh
exec 2>&1
wait_dep() {
    sv start "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    i=0
    until sv check "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; do
        i=$((i+1))
        [ "$i" -ge 90 ] && { echo "dependency $1 not ready after 90s" >&2; exit 1; }
        sleep 1
    done
}
/usr/local/libexec/3tched/opdbus-rundirs-up
install -d -m 0755 /run/opdbus/runit-ready
touch /run/opdbus/runit-ready/opdbus-rundirs
exec pause
check
finish
log
run

# Incus container runit services

Generator: `3tched-incus-svcgen` (installed at `/usr/local/bin/3tched-incus-svcgen`).

```sh
# one container
sudo 3tched-incus-svcgen mail-3tched

# all named workload CTs (skips UUID identity containers)
sudo 3tched-incus-svcgen --all-named

# define only, do not enable/start
sudo 3tched-incus-svcgen assistant --no-enable
```

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `/etc/runit/sv/incus-ct-<name>/` | service def (`run`, `check`, `finish`, `log/run`) |
| `/etc/runit/runsvdir/default/incus-ct-<name>` | enabled symlink |
| `/var/log/op-dbus/incus-ct-<name>/current` | svlogd logs (`s6log` user) |

Manage with standard runit:

```sh
sv status incus-ct-mail-3tched
sv restart incus-ct-netmaker
tail -F /var/log/op-dbus/incus-ct-mail-3tched/current
```

`boot.autostart` is forced off so **runit** owns lifecycle (not Incus).

    echo "starting container $NAME"

i=0
until incus list -f csv -c ns 2>/dev/null | grep -q "^${NAME},RUNNING$"; do

    echo "stopping container $NAME (runit down)"
    incus stop "$NAME" --timeout 30 2>/dev/null || incus stop "$NAME" --force 2>/dev/null || true
}
trap cleanup TERM INT HUP

# stay up while CT is RUNNING; exit 1 so runit restarts if CT dies under us
while incus list -f csv -c ns 2>/dev/null | grep -q "^${NAME},RUNNING$"; do

#!/bin/sh
# runit oneshot: bring identity-centric containers up from their own devices
# (OD-86). It runs after incusd because each identity's root is mounted into
# Incus's private pool path. A failed identity is logged and skipped; it
# never holds back incusd or any other container.
exec 2>&1

wait_dep() {
    sv start "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    i=0
    until sv check "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; do
        i=$((i + 1))
        [ "$i" -ge 90 ] && { echo "dependency $1 not ready after 90s" >&2; exit 1; }
        sleep 1
    done
}

wait_dep incusd

i=0
until incus info >/dev/null 2>&1; do
    i=$((i + 1))
    if [ "$i" -ge 60 ]; then
        echo "incusd API not ready" >&2
        exit 1
    fi
    sleep 1
done

/usr/local/libexec/3tched/op-identity-root up
/usr/local/libexec/3tched/op-identity-root status
/usr/local/libexec/3tched/runit-ready-signal identity-roots
exec pause
EOF

#!/bin/sh
[ -f /run/opdbus/runit-ready/identity-roots ]
EOF

rm -f /run/opdbus/runit-ready/identity-roots
EOF

The proper version is ready in source, committed as `36ea8e0` on `main`, not pushed:
- **`op-identity-root`** now lives with the release helpers, and `build-golden.sh` stages it. It defaults to the release's `/usr/local/bin/threetched-fs`.
- **`identity-roots` service:** at boot it waits for `incusd`, then brings every identity up from its device. Stopping the service never takes identities down.
- **`incus-ct-chatbot` service:** keeps the transitional chatbot running from boot, so the bridge always has its session.
- **The new `threetched-fs` binary** ships through the release's existing "stage every built executable" step. No list to update.

Already done on the host, since these aren't release-managed:
- **The old `threetched-fs` service** has a `down` file, so it stays off at boot and won't crash-loop.
- **`/etc/fstab`** mounts Raccoon by its UUID, and the two dead seed binds are commented out. It checks clean with 0 errors, and the backup is `/etc/fstab.bak-20260927`.

To make boot fully hands-off, these pieces need a release. That's the usual operator path: a workspace release build, `opblob seal-shm` and `persist`, `build-golden.sh`, snapshot, `btrfs send/receive`, and activation, which links the two new services and enables them. Until then, a reboot would still need `sudo /srv/git/odbus-verified/deploy/runit/libexec-3tched/op-identity-root up` with `THREETCHED_FS` pointed at the workspace build, plus starting the chatbot by hand.

The release build is workspace-wide cargo. If you want the Rust 2024 upgrade to ship in the same release, now is a good time to do it first. Just say "workspace" and whether to include 2024.

content.text:
The first-pass rewrites are all the conservative, behavior-preserving kind:
- **`if let … else` became `match`.** In 2024, a temporary in an `if let` is dropped before the `else` branch runs, and the `match` form keeps the old 2021 timing exactly. That matters where the temporary is a lock guard. The result looks awkward (`} _ => {` … `}}`), but the 2024 formatting pass will tidy it.
- **Macro fragments `$x:expr` became `$x:expr_2021`,** because in 2024 `expr` also matches `const { … }` and `_`. This keeps the macros matching exactly what they did before.
- **`Some(ref x)` became `Some(x)`,** where the reference is already implied. That's required by 2024's pattern rules and means the same thing.

The rerun is still going. I'll continue when it reports.

Two things are running in the background: the 2024 `/verify`, and the accountability trace.

When the trace comes back, there will probably be a decision that's yours. Filling this host's Qdrant for the demo means using the manual origin exception, which your design reserves for deliberate use. I'll bring the exact command and what it would fill, so you can decide.

message.content: mmanual origin?

content.text:
"Origin" here means **this server**: the machine where mutations happen and the hash chain is written. Your design (OD-64) splits the vector work in two:

1. **On the origin (here):** every committed chain event is turned into a vector right away, but the vector is only stored in the btrfs `vectors/` subvolume, next to the chain. The origin never writes chain vectors into its own Qdrant.
2. **On a replica (another machine):** you `btrfs send/receive` the snapshots over, and the replica loads those vectors into *its* Qdrant. That's where semantic search over the chain is meant to run.

The point is that the control plane never waits on the search index. If Qdrant or the embedder is down, mutations still land, and indexing catches up on the replica.

The **manual origin exception** is a deliberate override: the environment switch `OPDBUS_CHAIN_VECTORS_UPSERT_ORIGIN=1` (or an `--upsert-qdrant` flag) makes this server also write chain vectors into its own Qdrant. The design keeps it for manual use only, so it never happens by accident.

Why it matters for the demo: the trial view needs a Qdrant it can search. If no replica exists yet, the only option is to use the exception here once and load the 84,946 vectors into this host's Qdrant.

Is there a replica running anywhere, or is this server the only one right now?

message.content: we will just have the recieve subvolume be local

content.text:
That fits the design: the local received subvolume plays the replica's role. The flow becomes:
1. Snapshot the `vectors/` subvolume read-only.
2. `btrfs send | btrfs receive` it into a local receive location.
3. Run the replica-side ingest, which loads Qdrant from the **received** copy.

Qdrant only ever gets fed from a received snapshot, exactly as intended, with no second machine and no need for the manual exception.

The trace will give me the exact ingest command. Meanwhile, finding the live `vectors` subvolume:

The pieces are already there. The live chain is under `/var/lib/opdbus/snowball/` (`timing`, `vectors`, `state`), and the system already takes **aligned read-only snapshot sets**, up to at least `SNP-000109`, each with timing, vectors and state. 1. `btrfs send` the latest `SNP-…/vectors` (plus its timing and state, if the ingest needs them) into a local receive location, say `/var/lib/opdbus-replica/`.
2. Run the replica ingest against that received copy, which fills Qdrant's chain collection.
3. Point the Accountability search at it and check that results come back.

message.content: you think we should reset the vectors or the history (through many devleopment cycles) is useful

content.text:
Keep them. I'd separate the two things, though:

**The chain history: never reset it.** It's the hash-chained ledger itself, and your disaster recovery rebuilds from it. It's also the whole point of the Accountability view: a trial needs a record the agent couldn't rewrite, and 84,946 blocks spanning many development cycles is a strong demo of exactly that.

**The vectors: keep them too, though here it's a practical call.** They're derived from the chain, so they could always be rebuilt, but rebuilding means re-embedding 85k entries, which costs time and Voyage API money for nothing. The only good reason to rebuild would be if the embedding model or the text format changed partway through, so that old and new vectors no longer compare meaningfully. The Voyage 4 models share one 1024-dimension space, so that's probably not an issue, but I'll check it during ingest.

The real concern is **noise in the demo**: failed test runs, retired plugins like Netmaker, identities that no longer exist. Filtering at search time handles that better than a reset. The design already puts time, plugin and identity metadata in each vector's filterable fields, so the trial view can search, say, just the chatbot's session over the last few days, while the full history stays there as the permanent record.

So the plan: keep everything, ingest it all into the local replica, and give the demo's searches sensible default scope.

<result>## 1. UI — Accountability mode

Accountability is just one value of `ChatMode` (`/srv/git/3tched.com/src/chat/chat-mode.ts:15,21`, `"Ledger view; memory is read-only"`). There is **no dedicated Episodes table or search form** anywhere in the UI repo (`grep -rn accountability src` outside tests finds only this enum). Selecting it (`ModeStrip.tsx:141-160`) calls `project.select_context({mode:"accountability"})` (`chat-mode.ts:81-84`, `PROJECT_PLUGIN`/`CHAT_CONTEXT`), which returns a `ResolvedChatContext {memory_namespace, read_only, ...}`. Every subsequent turn goes through the **same generic chat box**: `door-chat-adapter.ts:submit()` (line ~245) calls `tched_router.Chat` with `{message, messages, provider, model}` — the same call every mode uses (only `control_plane` skips sending `provider`/`model`, so accountability still ships the dashboard's route selection, not `openrouter/auto`, a UI/backend mismatch vs. SIGNALS OD-69/OD-83). Rendering is the ordinary chat transcript; nothing reads or displays raw episodes or ledger rows client-side.

## 2. Backend — accountability handling & where "semantic search" happens

- `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/project_dispatch.rs:491-497`: `ChatMode::Accountability` sets `memory_namespace = "session/{s}/accountability"` and grants only `chat.context` + `snowball.read` (audit-trail reads: `query_events`/`verify_chain` in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/snowball_plugin.rs:493-520` — the actual "ledger", never wired to any UI table).
- `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/memory_binding.rs:13,72-74,207-213`: accountability's namespace is bound read-only — `memory_store`/`memory_delete` are refused; `memory_query`/`memory_semantic_query` are allowed.
- `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/chat_mode_routing.rs:19-20,29-33`: accountability gets a dedicated native router alias (`ACCOUNTABILITY_AGENT`), not the user's dashboard model — `tched_router_runtime.rs:2413-2438` shows it's pinned to provider profile `openrouter.accountability` (OpenRouter Auto per SIGNALS/WISHLIST OD-69).
- **Semantic search actually happens in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/context_bundle.rs`** (`assemble_for_context`, lines 136-225), injected as a system message before every `tched_router.Chat` completion:
  - Step 1: lexical episode recall from Cozo via `ctl_plane_chatbot_episode_cozo().list_scoped_episodes(...)` (line 156) — keyword match, not vector.
  - Step 3 `semantic_recall()` (lines 227-276): if `runtime.qdrant_shuttle()` is configured, calls the `cognitive_memory` MCP tool with `{operation:"semantic_query", query, namespace: context.memory_namespace, container_id: namespace, limit:5}`.
  - That op (`crates/op-cognitive-mcp/src/cognitive_tools.rs:437-473`, `op_semantic_query`) embeds the query and calls `QdrantSemanticShuttle::search_user_memory(embedding, container_id, limit)` (`qdrant_shuttle.rs:264-292`) — **this queries the `user_memory` collection, filtered by `container_id = "session/{s}/accountability"`, not `ctl_plane_reasoning_episodes`.**
  - `qdrant_shuttle.rs:129-208` (`fetch_trace_episodes`/`search_semantic_trace`, doc'd "Accountability Loop fetched semantic trace episodes") reads `ctl_plane_reasoning_episodes` (`DEFAULT_COLLECTION_NAME`), but nothing in the chat path calls these — the only caller is the gRPC `search_semantic_trace` RPC, which is stubbed to always fail (`crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/grpc_server.rs:2033-2041`: `"semantic trace search requires a canonical caller-scoped method contract"`). `crates/op-web/src/handlers/analytics.rs:49-66` (`GET /api/analytics/semantic-search`) is likewise an explicit TODO stub returning empty results — registered in `op-web/src/routes/mod.rs:180` but never called by the UI (grep found nothing in 3tched.com).

## 3. Who writes `ctl_plane_reasoning_episodes` / `user_memory`

- **`ctl_plane_reasoning_episodes` is never written by anything in this codebase.** `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/ctl_plane_chatbot.rs:36-39` states explicitly: `qdrant_collection` is a "Reserved legacy collection label; no Qdrant episode index is implemented," and other fields on the same config (`dedup_window_hrs`, `queue_alert_threshold`, `nesting_policy`) are marked "Reserved legacy value ... not implemented." `QdrantSemanticShuttle` never calls `create_collection`/`ensure_collection` for it (only `ChainVectorIndex` does, for a different collection) — matching it being absent live.
- **`user_memory`** is written by `mirror_semantic_memory` (`cognitive_tools.rs:522-565`), fired only when a `memory_store` call carries `{"semantic": true}` — but accountability mode blocks all `memory_store` calls (read-only), so nothing seeds `container_id="session/{s}/accountability"` there today. The other writer, `op-chat`'s `memory_loop.rs:380-410` (`upsert_user_memory`), belongs to a separate, legacy op-web chat surface (`op-web/src/handlers/tched_router.rs:174,285` tells callers to use the :8090 bridge instead) — not the live door path per AGENTS.md's "one public MCP door" invariant. So `user_memory` is also, in practice, unpopulated for accountability.
- Actual episode *vectorization* happens generically, not per-collection: OD-64's `ChainVectorProjector` (`crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/chain_vector_projector.rs`) embeds every committed chain block — including the chatbot's own `episode_committed`/`knowledge_committed` signals (declared in `ctl_plane_chatbot.rs:820,828`) — into the Snowball `vectors/` subvolume automatically, origin or replica, via `SchemaProjectionPolicy`. Qdrant writes are separate (see §4).

## 4. Chain vectors / OD-64 manual exception

`crates/op-cognitive-mcp/src/chain_vectors.rs:1-28` documents the invariant: automatic `project_pending(upsert_qdrant=false)` embeds into the chain only; Qdrant (`snowball_footprints`, `DEFAULT_COLLECTION` at line 45) is filled automatically only on a **replica** after `btrfs receive` (`ingest_received`). Two manual exceptions exist, both env/flag gated, no `CallMethod` flag:
1. **`OPDBUS_CHAIN_VECTORS_UPSERT_ORIGIN=1`** (`chain_vector_projector.rs:178-179,204`) — read once at bridge startup; makes the always-running projector call `project_pending(..., upsert_qdrant=true)` going forward. **Does not backfill the existing 84,946 blocks** — `project_pending` only processes blocks with `!has_vector`, and those are already embedded.
2. **CLI `op-chain-vectors project --limit N --upsert-qdrant`** (`bin/op-chain-vectors.rs:44-57,113-121`) — same limitation as above (only new/pending blocks).
3. **The command that actually backfills**: **`op-chain-vectors reindex`** → `ChainVectorIndex::open_replica().reindex_from_chain()` (`chain_vectors.rs:400-448`) — iterates every already-vectorized block and upserts it into `snowball_footprints` directly from the chain, no Voyage key, no send/receive. This is the documented "operator catch-up" path for exactly the 84,946-blocks-already-embedded scenario.

**Does Accountability search read `snowball_footprints`?** No. `ChainVectorIndex::search()` (`chain_vectors.rs:586`) is only invoked from the `op-chain-vectors search` CLI subcommand — it is not exposed via any D-Bus plugin method, gRPC service, or MCP tool, so nothing in `context_bundle.rs`/`tched_router.Chat` can reach it. This is the core code gap.

## 5. Shortest demo path, and AGENTS.md risk

content.text:
Here's the chain-history vectorization logic as it stands, for your review. It's the OD-64 code: `chain_vector_projector.rs`, `chain_vectors.rs`, and `op-snowball`.

**1. When it runs.** Every committed mutation becomes a Snowball chain block. The projector on this host wakes up and embeds any new blocks in batches. It never blocks the control plane: if the embedder is down, embedding just catches up later.

**2. What text gets embedded for each block.**
```
block: 42000
plugin: identity_sled
action: record_session_event
plugin: Identity Sled — <the plugin's description from its sealed schema>
method: record_session_event
subid: mut.service.identity-sled.session-event.record@v1
kind (Event kind, e.g. "arrival"…): arrival
content (JSON payload of the event.): {...}
```
- The sealed schema filters out noise. Only the method's or signal's **declared arguments** are embedded, each labelled with the schema author's own description. Fields marked `x-secret` are dropped, and undeclared keys are ignored.
- Values are cut at 512 characters. For a retired plugin with no sealed schema, only the three header lines get embedded.

**3. Where it goes.** Each block's vector is stored as `vec-<block>.bin` (1,024 floats) with a `.meta.json` recording timing and host load, inside the chain's `vectors/` subvolume. That's where your 84,946 are.

**4. What travels with each vector into Qdrant** (on the replica or local receive, into `snowball_footprints`): block number, event hash, input hash, plugin, action, timestamp, `actor_id`, `session_id`, `sealed_id_digest`, `capability_id`, `decision`, subid, schema version and the text. Each vector's ID is fixed by its block number, so re-ingesting overwrites rather than duplicating.

**What I'd flag in the review:**
- **Outcomes aren't embedded, only inputs.** Whether a call was allowed or denied is only in the metadata, not in the embedded text, and results and errors aren't anywhere. A trial question like "why did it fail?" or "what did it change?" needs the outcome in the text.
- **The block number is in the text.** It carries no meaning, and it makes otherwise-identical events look less similar to each other.
- **Who acted is only in the metadata.** `actor_id` is there for filtering, but the text never says whether it was the chatbot or you, and that's exactly what the trial view asks about.
- **Changing the text means re-embedding** all 85k blocks with Voyage. So settle the text before the first ingest.

**Where filling the Cozo graph fits:** in the same ingest step as Qdrant, running on the **received copy**. That way the origin still never waits on it, and the graph stays derived from the chain and can be rebuilt at any time (keyed by event hash, so ingesting twice is safe). Each block would add:
- **Nodes:** the event, who acted (principal and session), the plugin, the method (subid) and the capability.
- **Edges:** *actor performed event*; *event invoked method*; *event required capability*; *event decided Allow or Deny*; *event follows the previous event*.
- Later, *method satisfies control*, from your OSCAL tag rules, which connects the chain straight to compliance.

These would go into the `graph_node` and `graph_edge` relations Cozo already has.

The knowledge vectors (compliance, code and docs) are a separate pipeline, and I'd review them separately.

For the chain side, three decisions:
1. Add outcomes and the actor's role to the embedded text, and drop the block number?
2. Build the graph at ingest, on the received copy?
3. Re-embed the 85k blocks before the first ingest?

Agreed on both, and the order makes sense: **knowledge first, chain history after**, once the embedding text is settled. The drop-in apps (a CMS, Slack, whatever someone needs) are the strongest thing to show on Oct 1. "Tell it what you need, and a working app appears, built from your schema under your rules" is exactly what makes people lean in.

Here's where each piece stands and what it depends on.

**Knowledge.** The vectors mostly exist already: `compliance_general` (85,989) and `compliance_official` (3,697) are in Qdrant. What's missing is:
1. **The rest of your vectorizing.** I don't know where that runs. The scripts in the repo point at paths that don't exist on this host. Where is it, and what's left?
2. **The Cozo graph.** Controls become nodes, OSCAL `required` and `related` links become edges, and framework and source nodes get added too. The parsing is straightforward, since the control ID and links are right in each chunk. One constraint, though: **Cozo is held open by the bridge**, so nothing else can write it directly. Writes have to go through the bridge, either a `cozo.run_query` call made with a credential, or an ingest step inside the bridge that ships in a release. That's the same credential question the lungs hit. I'd do it as a bridge-side ingest, like the chain's.

**The drop-in apps demo** depends on one thing: **connected chat working from your machine**. The chatbot's UI-render mode is what builds those apps, and I still can't test your decoy hop from here. Once you open `http://10.0.0.4:8080/demo/` over your tunnel, we'll know within a minute whether it's live or exactly which hop fails.

With three days left, I'd order it like this:
1. **Today:** you run the `/demo/` test. I finish the 2024 upgrade (the check is still running) and write the knowledge-graph ingest.
2. **Next:** generate and refine two or three drop-in apps live (CMS, a Slack-like channel app, a compliance dashboard), ideally with compliance rules attached from the knowledge graph.
3. **Before Oct 1:** a release, so it all survives a reboot.

Where's your knowledge vectorizer running, and what's still left to do?

content.text:
Good idea, and it removes the credential problem. With the bridge stopped, its hold on Cozo is released, so an offline tool can write the knowledge graph directly. The natural time is the **release window**: activation already takes the bridge down (`sv down … op-grpc-bridge …`). So:
1. Stop services for the release.
2. Run the knowledge ingest: read the knowledge vectors from Qdrant, parse the OSCAL controls and their links, and write them into Cozo's graph.
3. Activate the release and bring everything back.

No door and no credential needed, and nothing runs concurrently with the live bridge.

I'll build it as a small Rust tool that **refuses to run while the bridge holds Cozo**, has a dry-run mode that just prints what it would write, and is safe to rerun: each node is keyed by control ID and source, so a second run overwrites rather than duplicates.

content.text:
It's implemented, but it's narrower than the demo needs:
- **UI:** "UI render" is in the mode picker ("Explore candidate interfaces; no memory read or written").
- **Model instructions:** in that mode the model is told to propose designs as one json-render canvas built only from the app's validated components. That's how your CMS came out.
- **Backend:** the mode gets no memory and only the `chat.context` capability, which is deliberate.

Two gaps separate that from "compliant drop-in apps":
1. **Generated canvases are static by rule.** The instructions allow "only static props… no actions, bindings", and the output is labelled a *proposal for review*. So a generated CMS is a design, not a working app. Wiring it to real methods goes through your gallery → catalog review.
2. **The mode can't look up compliance, and it shouldn't.** If the model wrote the controls, they'd be made up.

The clean fix keeps the model out of the compliance claim entirely:
- **The model marks intent:** each component that represents an operation carries the method it would call as a plain static field, e.g. *"Publish" → `project.publish_document`*.
- **The platform attaches compliance:** the UI looks up each of those methods' `control_refs` through the door, and shows them beside the canvas, with the trace method → control → spec release.

The compliance comes from the registry and the graph, not from the model, so it's deterministic and traceable. That's the claim that holds up in front of reviewers.

The work:
- **UI:** an optional method field on the relevant components, plus a compliance panel.
- **Backend:** the lookup, using the OSCAL registry's existing read methods.
- **Data:** the `control_refs` for the demo apps' methods, plus the control graph.

The generated app stays a design until it's reviewed and promoted. For Oct 1, the honest pitch is *"designed on demand, compliance-mapped by the platform"*, with live wiring as the next step. Does that framing work for you?

content.text:
As a generated design from a one-line prompt: **about 8/10**. As an actual CMS: **about 3/10**, because it's a CMS *dashboard*, not a CMS.

**What's genuinely good:**
- **Sensible domain model:** four content types that make sense (Editorial Article, Landing Page, Release Note, Policy Document), each with a handle, version, field count and status.
- **Governance instincts without any OSCAL.** The publishing pipeline is *draft validation* ("validate field types, required values, references, and schema version before review") → *two-person review* ("an editor other than the author") → a *policy gate* → publish. That's separation of duties and change control, arrived at on its own.
- **It understood your architecture.** *"No parallel schema authority is introduced by this module"* is your one-truth rule, unprompted. It mounts under Schema Control, and it uses the live schema renderer, registry stream and catalog index for real system data.
- **It's honest about what's fake.** *"Live schema data remains authoritative; the editorial records below are seeded preview content."*

**What holds it back:**
- **Its content types are invented,** not derived from your schema. That was the bar you set, and it didn't meet it. There's no CMS plugin for it to derive from, so it made plausible fiction and labelled it as such.
- **It's a dashboard of a CMS:** there's no editor for an entry, no field definitions (just counts like "14 fields"), no media, no roles, no version history.
- **It's static** and was built on the old component catalog, so it won't render today without regenerating it.

**What OSCAL would add** is traceability for instincts it already has:

| Stage | NIST 800-53 control |
|---|---|
| Draft validation | SI-10, information input validation |
| Two-person review | AC-5, separation of duties, and CM-3, change control |
| Approval evidence | AU-2 / AU-12, audit events |
| The retention policy document | SI-12, information retention |

So the pitch writes itself: *the generator already designs with good governance instincts, and OSCAL turns each instinct into a named, sourced control.* That's the "compliant from the start" demo.

content.text:
An extension, mostly. The hard parts of a CMS already exist in your platform as general building blocks:

| A CMS needs | What already exists |
|---|---|
| Content types with fields | A `cms` plugin whose **schema declares them**. The plugin *is* the schema, which also fixes the generated design's invented types. |
| Storing entries | The `project` plugin's documents (`put_document`, `list_documents`), scoped to a project |
| Who can edit | Project membership (`invite`, `accept_invite`, `revoke_member`) plus per-principal capability grants |
| Validation before review | Every call is already checked against the sealed schema |
| Version history | Every edit is a MutationEngine commit, so it's on the chain automatically |
| Two-person review | One server-side rule: the approver's verified identity must differ from the author's. The door already verifies identity. |
| Approval evidence and audit | The ledger, which is exactly what the Accountability view reads |
| Notifications | The mail plugin and the EMQX doorbell |
| Screens | Generated in UI-render mode, then reviewed and promoted |

So the core is **one new plugin** composed from those parts. Content types, entries and the pipeline methods (`create_entry`, `submit_for_review`, `approve`, `publish`) come to maybe a few days of focused work.

Three things would be real stretches:
1. **Media and file storage.** There's no asset store yet, so images and attachments need a design, probably per-project storage on btrfs.
2. **Public publishing.** Your system is built to be invisible, and serving published pages to the internet needs a deliberate public edge. That's an architecture decision, not just code.
3. **An editing component.** The UI catalog has no rich-text editor yet, only form previews.

For Oct 1 I wouldn't build it, since the three days are already spoken for. It does make a strong line for the demo, though: *"the CMS you just watched get generated is one plugin away from working, because documents, versions, roles, review and audit are already platform primitives."*
